tapset: Captive-bred stock usually adapts to San Diego tap water with slow acclimation. For best color and health, many keepers blend tap with RO/DI water.
Prefers softer, more acidic water than San Diego's tap (pH roughly 7.6-8.6, hard). Most keepers blend tap with RO/DI water or use a remineralized RO/DI supply.
Naturally suited to San Diego's hard, alkaline tap water once it is dechlorinated (the city uses chloramine, so use a conditioner that handles it).
Tolerates San Diego's hard, alkaline tap water (pH roughly 7.6-8.6) with slow acclimation and a conditioner that handles chloramine.

items.name: Neon Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets and flakes
items.note: A small, calm schooling fish that shows its best color in a group of six or more. Captive-bred fish are hardier than wild ones, but they still prefer stable water over big swings.
tips: Add them after the tank has fully cycled.
Keep 6 or more so they school instead of hiding.
Avoid big, mouthy tankmates that see them as snacks.

items.name: Cardinal Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: Larger and more brilliantly colored than a neon, with a red stripe along the whole belly. Likes warm, clean, slightly soft water and a planted tank with some shade.
tips: Prefers warmer water than neons (upper 70s).
Dim lighting and floating plants make them bolder.
Feed small amounts; they are shy at feeding time.

items.name: Ember Tetra
items.diet: Micro pellets, crushed flakes, baby brine shrimp
items.note: A tiny, glowing orange tetra that is ideal for nano planted tanks. Because of its size, tankmates need to be gentle and small-mouthed.
tips: Great with shrimp and other nano fish.
Feed tiny foods they can actually swallow.
Choose a tight-fitting lid; they can jump.

items.name: Black Skirt Tetra
items.origin: Paraguay and Parana basins, South America
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A hardy, active tetra that tolerates a wide range of conditions. Keep it in a group to reduce fin-nipping, and avoid pairing it with long-finned fish like bettas or angelfish.
tips: A larger group spreads out any nipping.
Skip slow, long-finned tankmates.

items.name: Lemon Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A soft yellow tetra with a bright red eye. Easy to keep and good in community tanks with similar-sized fish.
tips: Looks best in a group in a planted tank.
Stable water matters more than exact numbers.

items.name: Rummy Nose Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: A tight-schooling tetra that is a classic indicator of water quality: a pale red nose means something is off. Likes warm, very clean water.
tips: Keep 8 or more; they school tightly.
Do frequent small water changes.
Add only to a mature, stable tank.

items.name: Congo Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A larger, shimmering tetra whose fins lengthen as males mature. Needs open swimming room and a gentle current.
tips: Needs a longer tank for swimming.
Slow, long-finned fish may get harassed.
Keep a group of six or more.

items.name: Harlequin Rasbora
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A calm, copper-colored school fish with a black triangle. One of the most reliable community fish for planted tanks.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Do well with small peaceful tankmates and shrimp.

items.name: Chili Rasbora
items.diet: Micro foods: crushed flakes, baby brine shrimp
items.note: A tiny, deep-red nano fish that needs a calm, planted tank and equally gentle tankmates. Shy at first, bolder in a larger group.
tips: Pair with other nano fish and shrimp.
Offer food small enough to swallow.
Tight lid; small fish still jump.

items.name: Celestial Pearl Danio
items.diet: Micro pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: Also called the galaxy rasbora. Males show spangled orange fins and females are plumper and paler. Peaceful and small, but shy until they feel secure.
tips: Plants and floating cover help them settle in.
Keep a group with a good mix of males and females.

items.name: Zebra Danio
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A fast, hardy school fish that tolerates cooler water. Great for cycling-friendly community tanks, but too busy for very shy or slow tankmates.
tips: Keep 6 or more.
Not the best match for long-finned bettas or slow fish.
Needs a tight lid.

items.name: White Cloud Mountain Minnow
items.diet: Flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A cool-water school fish that is happy without a heater in most homes. A good choice for unheated tanks and for pairing with hardy, cooler-water species.
tips: Tolerates cooler room temperatures.
Best in groups of six or more.

items.name: Cherry Barb
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A gentle, red barb that is far calmer than other barbs. Males color up when they have females and cover to display around.
tips: Keep more females than males.
Dense planting makes them bolder.

items.name: Tiger Barb
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: Active and bold, with a reputation for nipping. Large groups spread out the aggression, and they should not be kept with long-finned or slow fish.
tips: Keep at least 8 so they pick on each other, not tankmates.
Avoid bettas, angelfish and gouramis.

items.name: Boesemani Rainbowfish
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A colorful, active schooling fish that colors up slowly over the first year. Likes hard, alkaline water, which suits San Diego tap water well.
tips: Needs swimming room: a longer tank.
Color develops with age and good care.

items.name: Guppy
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: Hardy, colorful livebearers that breed readily. Keep more females than males to reduce harassment, and plan for fry.
tips: Two or three females per male.
They breed fast; be ready for babies.
Like hard, alkaline water.

items.name: Endler's Livebearer
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets
items.note: A small, vivid relative of the guppy. A bit more nano-friendly, but equally prolific.
tips: Keep more females than males.
Will interbreed with guppies.

items.name: Platy
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, veggie foods
items.note: A cheerful, easy livebearer in many colors. Good for new keepers who have hard water.
tips: Keep more females than males.
Add some vegetable-based food.

items.name: Molly
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, algae, veggie foods
items.note: A hardy livebearer that likes hard, alkaline water and a little vegetable matter in its diet. Some keepers add a little aquarium salt, but it is not required for most freshwater tanks.
tips: Needs hard, alkaline water.
Offer algae wafers or blanched veggies.

items.name: Swordtail
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, veggie foods
items.note: An active livebearer named for the male's sword-like tail extension. Needs a longer tank and a tight lid.
tips: Keep one male with several females.
Needs a tight lid; they jump.

items.name: Panda Cory
items.diet: Sinking pellets, wafers, frozen foods
items.note: A small, black-and-white armored catfish that likes soft sand and company. Prefers slightly cooler water than many tropical fish.
tips: Use sand or smooth gravel to protect their barbels.
Keep 6 or more.
Make sure sinking food reaches them.

items.name: Bronze Cory
items.diet: Sinking pellets, wafers, frozen foods
items.note: A hardy, long-lived cory that tolerates a wide range of water. A reliable clean-up crew member for community tanks.
tips: Keep 6 or more.
Feed sinking foods after lights dim.

items.name: Kuhli Loach
items.diet: Sinking pellets, frozen and live foods
items.note: An eel-like, nocturnal loach that hides in plants and leaf litter. Needs soft sand and plenty of cover, and a tightly covered tank because they escape through tiny gaps.
tips: Use sand, not sharp gravel.
Cover every gap; they escape.
Feed after lights out.

items.name: Clown Loach
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets, frozen foods, snails
items.note: A famous, long-lived loach that gets much larger than the juveniles sold. Needs a big tank and a group, and can be sensitive to ich.
tips: Plan for a very large tank at full size.
Quarantine new fish; they are ich-prone.
Provide caves and wood.

items.name: Bristlenose Pleco
items.diet: Algae, sinking wafers, blanched veggies, driftwood
items.note: The small, practical pleco. Stays far smaller than common plecos and munches algae and biofilm. Needs driftwood to graze on.
tips: Always keep driftwood in the tank.
Males can be territorial with each other.
Supplement with veggie wafers.

items.name: Otocinclus
items.level: Mid to bottom (on plants and glass)
items.diet: Algae and biofilm; supplement with veggie wafers
items.note: A tiny algae-grazing catfish that does best in a mature, planted tank with a steady supply of biofilm. Often fragile when newly imported.
tips: Add only to a tank with visible algae or biofilm.
Supplement with veggie foods.
Keep a group of 4 or more.

items.name: Siamese Algae Eater
items.temperament: Peaceful, can chase its own kind
items.diet: Algae, flakes, pellets, veggies
items.note: A busy grazer that eats some types of algae. Active and fast, and best in a longer tank with current. Be careful to buy the true species, not look-alikes.
tips: Needs a longer tank with some current.
Provide wood and plants for grazing.

items.name: Betta
items.diet: Carnivore: betta pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A bold, long-finned labyrinth fish that breathes air at the surface. Males cannot share a tank with one another. Needs a heated, filtered tank, not a bowl.
tips: Heater and gentle filter, not a bowl.
Never house two males together.
Avoid fin-nipping tankmates.

items.name: Dwarf Gourami
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A colorful, calm gourami that is prone to a viral disease in commercial stock. Choose healthy fish and quarantine carefully.
tips: Buy only active, clear-finned fish.
Quarantine new arrivals.
One male per tank unless it is large and well planted.

items.name: Honey Gourami
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A small, mellow gourami that is hardier than dwarfs. A good centerpiece for a peaceful nano tank with floating plants.
tips: Floating plants help them feel safe.
Great with other small, calm fish.

items.name: Pearl Gourami
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: An elegant, gentle gourami with a lace-like pattern. Likes a planted tank with floating plants and calm tankmates.
tips: Floating plants make them more confident.
Avoid boisterous fin-nippers.

items.name: Blue Gourami (Three Spot)
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A big, hardy gourami that can be pushy with smaller or similar-shaped fish. Better in a larger, well-planted tank.
tips: Males can be aggressive with each other.
Needs a larger tank than small gouramis.

items.name: German Blue Ram
items.diet: Micro pellets, frozen and live foods
items.note: A jewel-like dwarf cichlid that likes warm, clean, soft-to-moderate water. Delicate compared with most community fish, so buy healthy stock and keep conditions steady.
tips: Needs warm, very stable water.
Buy tank-raised, healthy fish.
Provide caves and smooth sand.

items.name: Bolivian Ram
items.diet: Micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A hardier, larger cousin of the German blue ram that tolerates cooler water and wider conditions.
tips: Better first dwarf cichlid than the German ram.
Provide smooth sand and caves.

items.name: Cockatoo Apistogramma
items.diet: Micro pellets, frozen and live foods
items.note: A colorful, easier dwarf cichlid. Males set up territories and need caves and line-of-sight breaks. See our dedicated Apistogramma guide at apistogrammarama.com.
tips: Provide a cave per female.
Keep one male per tank unless it is large.
Use leaf litter, caves, plants.

items.name: Angelfish
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A tall, elegant cichlid that needs a tall tank. Small tetras like neons can end up as food once the angelfish is grown.
tips: Needs a tall tank.
Avoid tiny schooling fish like neons.
Avoid fin-nipping tankmates.

items.name: Discus
items.diet: Discus pellets, frozen and live foods
items.note: The 'king of the aquarium': a disc-shaped, warm-water cichlid that demands pristine water, high temperatures and frequent water changes. See our Discus Guides site for in-depth care.
tips: Needs very warm, very clean water.
Large, frequent water changes.
Feed several small meals, not one big one.

items.name: Oscar
items.diet: Carnivore: pellets, frozen foods
items.note: An intelligent, big, messy cichlid with a lot of personality. Needs a large tank and powerful filtration, and any fish that fits in its mouth will be eaten.
tips: Heavy bioload: oversize the filter.
Rearranges decor; secure heavy items.
Tank mates must be large and tough.

items.name: Convict Cichlid
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A hardy, prolific, feisty cichlid. A great first cichlid for a species tank, but tankmates will be bullied when it breeds.
tips: Best kept in a pair, alone or with large tough fish.
Provide caves.
Breeds easily.

items.name: Electric Yellow Lab
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets and veggie foods
items.note: A bright yellow Lake Malawi mbuna and one of the gentler ones. Needs hard, alkaline water and rockwork, and does best with other Malawi cichlids.
tips: Needs hard, alkaline water.
Stack rocks for caves, with sturdy placement.
Keep other Malawi fish, not tropical community fish.

items.name: Kribensis
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A small, colorful West African cichlid that is a classic cave-breeder and fiercely protective parent. Gets along with larger peaceful community fish.
tips: Provide caves such as half coconut shells.
Pairs defend the cave when breeding.

items.name: Jack Dempsey
items.diet: Carnivore: pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A hardy, blue-speckled Central American cichlid with a big attitude. Needs a large tank and strong filtration, and tankmates must be large and tough.
tips: Oversize the filter.
Tankmates must be big and robust.
Rearranges decor.

items.name: Flowerhorn Cichlid
items.diet: Carnivore: quality cichlid pellets, occasional frozen foods
items.note: A captive-bred hybrid known for its bold colors and prominent head hump. Intelligent, interactive and territorial: it needs its own large, well-filtered tank. See our dedicated Flowerhorn Hobby site.
tips: Keep alone.
Heavy bioload: strong filtration and big water changes.
Choose a sturdy glass or acrylic with a lid.

items.name: Pea Puffer
items.social: Solitary in 5 gal; groups in 15+ gal with lots of plants
items.diet: Carnivore: live and frozen foods; snails help wear their beak
items.note: The smallest puffer. Personable but nippy and a picky carnivore that needs snails, frozen foods and sometimes live foods.
tips: Needs live or frozen foods; no flakes.
Do not keep with fin-nipping-vulnerable tankmates.
Add plenty of plants for line of sight breaks.

items.name: Figure 8 Puffer
items.diet: Carnivore: snails, shrimp, frozen foods
items.note: A small, brackish puffer that needs salinity (specific gravity about 1.005-1.008) to stay healthy, plus a diet of hard-shelled foods to wear down its beak.
tips: Needs brackish water; do not keep in plain freshwater long-term.
Feed snails and shell-on foods.
Keep alone.

items.name: Fancy Goldfish
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking goldfish pellets, veggies
items.note: Round-bodied goldfish such as orandas, ranchus and fantails. Heavy waste producers that need big tanks and strong filtration, not bowls. See our goldfish vs. tropical fish guide for why they can't share with tropicals.
tips: Plan 30 gallons for the first fish plus 10-20 for each additional.
Strong filtration and weekly water changes.
Do not mix with tropical fish.

items.name: Comet Goldfish
items.diet: Omnivore: goldfish pellets, veggies
items.note: The classic long-bodied, single-tailed goldfish. Active and large, and best suited to a pond or a very large tank.
tips: Needs a pond or very large tank.
Heavy waste: strong filtration.
Do not keep with tropical fish.

items.name: Silver Arowana
items.diet: Carnivore: pellets, frozen fish and insects
items.note: A giant surface-dwelling predator that can jump straight through gaps in a lid. Needs a very large tank with a heavy, secure cover, and it will eat anything it can swallow.
tips: Secure, heavy lid; they jump.
Needs a very large tank as an adult.
Tankmates must be large enough not to be eaten.

items.name: Neocaridina Shrimp
items.diet: Biofilm, algae, shrimp pellets, blanched veggies
items.note: Cherry shrimp and other color morphs. Easy, active and breed readily in a planted tank, but sensitive to copper and some medications.
tips: Never use copper-based medications.
Add after the tank has cycled.
Acclimate slowly, with drip acclimation.

items.name: Amano Shrimp
items.diet: Algae, biofilm, shrimp pellets, blanched veggies
items.note: A larger, tireless algae grazer. They breed only in brackish water, so they will not overrun a freshwater tank.
tips: Acclimate slowly.
Great algae eaters.
Secure the lid; they can climb out.

items.name: Nerite Snail
items.diet: Algae and biofilm
items.note: A hard-working algae-eating snail that will not overrun a tank because its eggs rarely hatch in freshwater. Needs hard water with some calcium to keep its shell healthy, and a lid, because it climbs.
tips: Needs hard water for shell health.
Will leave small white eggs on hardscape.
Needs a secure lid.

items.name: Mystery Snail
items.diet: Algae, veggies, sinking pellets
items.note: A big, charismatic scavenger that breathes air at the surface and lays eggs above the waterline. Keep a gap at the top of the tank. It can also nibble delicate plants if underfed.
tips: Leave air space at the top.
Needs calcium in the water for shell health.
Feed veggies so plants are left alone.

items.name: African Dwarf Frog
items.diet: Carnivore: frozen bloodworms, brine shrimp, sinking frog pellets
items.note: A small, fully aquatic frog that needs a lid with an air gap because it surfaces to breathe. Its eyesight is poor, so it often loses out on food to fast tankmates.
tips: Use a lid with a small air gap and no open edges.
Feed sinking foods or target-feed with a pipette.
Do not mix with large or fast fish; keep calm tankmates.
aka: dwarf zaire platinum african dwarf frog

items.name: Fire Belly Newt
items.diet: Carnivore: frozen bloodworms, blackworms, sinking carnivore pellets
items.note: A hardy, mostly aquatic newt with a bright orange belly that likes cool water. Provide a land area and a very secure lid, and wash your hands before and after handling anything in the tank.
tips: Keep it cool; avoid temperatures above the low 70s.
Provide a land area or floating perch and a tight lid.
Wash hands before and after touching the tank; its skin has mild toxins.

items.name: Paddletail Newt
items.diet: Carnivore: frozen bloodworms, blackworms, earthworms, sinking pellets
items.note: A large, mostly aquatic newt that needs cool, well-oxygenated water and plenty of hiding spots. It struggles in warm tanks, so a chiller or a cool room matters.
tips: Keep it cool, ideally under 70°F.
Provide caves and hiding spots.
Use a tight lid and strong filtration.

items.name: Spanish Ribbed Newt
items.diet: Carnivore: frozen bloodworms, earthworms, sinking pellets
items.note: A large, hardy, mostly aquatic newt that is easy to feed. When threatened it can push its ribs through its skin, so handle as little as possible and keep it away from small fish and shrimp.
tips: Keep it cool; avoid warm rooms.
Do not keep with small fish or shrimp.
Use a tight lid and some land or a floating perch.

items.name: Shovelnose Catfish
items.diet: Carnivore: frozen fish, shrimp, pellets
items.note: Tiger shovelnose and related catfish are sold small but grow into very large predators, often over three feet long. They eat any fish that fits in their mouths and need a huge tank, many hundreds of gallons for a tiger.
tips: Needs a very large tank; juveniles outgrow home tanks fast.
Do not keep with smaller fish.
aka: spotted hybrid tiger shovel nose catfish

items.name: Serpae Tetra
items.origin: Paraguay and Amazon basins, South America
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A bold red tetra that does best in a group of six or more, which spreads out its fin nipping. Keep it away from long-finned tankmates.
tips: Always keep a group; singles get nippy.
Pick fast, short-finned tankmates.

items.name: Bleeding Heart Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A deep-bodied tetra with a red spot behind the gill. Males grow tall, flowing dorsal fins. Likes warm, clean water and a planted tank.
tips: Give it a tank 30 gallons or larger.
Keep a group of six or more.

items.name: Buenos Aires Tetra
items.origin: Parana and Paraguay basins, South America
items.temperament: Active, may nip and eat plants
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, plant matter
items.note: A hardy, fast tetra that tolerates cooler water. It nibbles soft plants, so tough plants like anubias and java fern work best.
tips: Offer vegetable-based foods to reduce plant nibbling.
Needs swimming room.

items.name: X-Ray Tetra
items.origin: Guianas and Amazon basin, South America
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets
items.note: A hardy, translucent tetra whose skeleton shows through its skin. A forgiving first fish for a community tank.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Tolerates a range of water conditions.

items.name: Flame Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets
items.note: A small, hardy tetra with a red rear half. Tolerates cooler water than many tetras.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Good with other small, peaceful fish.

items.name: Diamond Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A sparkling, silvery tetra with glittering scales. Males develop longer fins as they mature.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Look best under moderate lighting with dark substrate.

items.name: Penguin Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets
items.note: A slim tetra that swims at a slight head-up angle, with a bold black stripe. Likes open swimming room.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Use a tight-fitting lid.

items.name: Black Phantom Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets
items.note: A small, calm tetra with a black body and a tall dorsal fin on males. Easy to keep with other peaceful community fish.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Stable, clean water brings out color.

items.name: Red Phantom Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets
items.note: A small tetra with a red body and a dark spot behind the gill. A peaceful, easy community fish.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Floating plants help them feel secure.

items.name: Bloodfin Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets
items.note: A hardy silver tetra with red fins that tolerates a wide temperature range. Active and quick, so give it swimming space.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Use a lid; they jump.

items.name: GloFish Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets
items.note: A brightly fluorescent, captive-bred variety of the black skirt tetra. Care is the same as for black skirt tetras; the color comes from selective breeding.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Blue or black lighting makes the glow stand out.

items.name: Emperor Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A calm tetra with a violet sheen and a blue eye. Males are larger and have longer center tail rays.
tips: Keep a small group with a few more females than males.
Gentle tankmates only.

items.name: Blue Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets
items.note: A silvery-blue schooling tetra with a calm temperament. Looks best in a group in a planted tank.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.

items.name: Bucktooth Tetra
items.origin: Guianas and Amazon basin, South America
items.diet: Carnivore leaning omnivore: pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A bold, active tetra that nips the fins and scales of tankmates. Best with fast, similar-sized fish in a roomy tank.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Avoid slow or long-finned tankmates.

items.name: Silver Tip Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets
items.note: A hardy, active tetra with white-tipped fins. A group keeps it busy and calm.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.

items.name: Hatchetfish
items.diet: Surface feeder: flies, small floating foods
items.note: Surface-dwelling fish with deep keel-shaped bellies that can jump out of the water. A tight lid and floating plants are essential.
tips: Use a very secure lid.
Feed small floating foods and live or frozen insects.
Keep a group of six or more.

items.name: Clown Rasbora
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A larger rasbora with a red-orange body and bold black spots. Needs a roomy, planted tank and soft, clean water.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Do regular water changes.

items.name: Strawberry Rasbora
items.diet: Micro pellets, baby brine shrimp, crushed flakes
items.note: A tiny, blush-red nano fish best kept with other small, peaceful species and shrimp. Prefers soft, clean, planted setups.
tips: Feed very small foods.
Keep a group of eight or more.

items.name: Pygmy Rasbora
items.diet: Micro pellets, baby brine shrimp
items.note: A tiny red-orange rasbora with a bold spot pattern, ideal for nano planted tanks.
tips: Keep a group of eight or more.
Pair with other tiny peaceful fish and shrimp.

items.name: Espei Rasbora
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets
items.note: A small orange rasbora with a dark wedge, closely related to the harlequin. Calm and easy in a planted community tank.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.

items.name: Emerald Dwarf Rasbora
items.diet: Micro pellets, baby brine shrimp, small frozen foods
items.note: A tiny rasbora with a blue-green sheen and orange fins. Needs peaceful tankmates and small foods.
tips: Feed tiny foods they can swallow.
Keep a group of eight or more.

items.name: Giant Danio
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A fast, hardy danio that needs a long tank and a tight lid. Great for active community tanks with similarly sized fish.
tips: Use a tight lid; they jump.
Give it a long tank for swimming.

items.name: Leopard Danio
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets
items.note: A spotted variety of the zebra danio. Hardy, active and easy, and tolerates cooler water.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Use a lid.

items.name: Rosy Barb
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, vegetables
items.note: A hardy barb that tolerates cooler tanks. Males flush rosy red when mature. Keep a group to calm any chasing.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Do not pair with slow, long-finned fish.

items.name: Odessa Barb
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets
items.note: A hardy barb whose males show a bright red band along the body. Active and easy to keep.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.

items.name: Ruby Barb
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, vegetables
items.note: A peaceful barb with a deep ruby head on breeding males. Does best in a planted tank with clean water.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.

items.name: Gold Barb
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, vegetables
items.note: A hardy, golden barb that tolerates cooler water. Good for unheated or lightly heated community tanks.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.

items.name: Denison Barb
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A fast, bright torpedo-shaped barb that likes a long tank with a current and plenty of oxygen.
tips: Give it a long tank and good flow.
Keep a group of six or more.

items.name: Tinfoil Barb
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, vegetables, frozen foods
items.note: A large, fast, silver schooling fish that outgrows most home tanks. It needs a very large aquarium and strong filtration.
tips: Plan for a large tank (125 gallons or more).
Eats soft plants.
Do not keep with small fish.

items.name: Melon Barb
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A peaceful, shoaling barb with a warm red-orange tone. Prefers a planted tank.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.

items.name: Bala Shark
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, frozen foods, vegetables
items.note: A silver, shark-shaped schooling fish that grows far larger than the juveniles sold in stores. It needs a very large, long tank.
tips: Plan for 180 gallons or more for a group.
Do not keep with small fish; they will be eaten.
Use a tight lid.

items.name: Rainbow Shark
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, algae wafers, frozen foods
items.note: A black bottom-dweller with red fins that guards its territory, especially against similar fish. Best kept one per tank.
tips: Keep only one per tank.
Provide caves and hiding spots.

items.name: Red Tail Black Shark
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, algae wafers, frozen foods
items.note: A velvet-black fish with a bright red tail. It claims a cave and chases other bottom fish, so it is usually kept alone.
tips: Keep only one per tank.
Provide caves and decor to break sight lines.

items.name: Flying Fox
items.diet: Omnivore: algae, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: An algae-eating fish with a black stripe and gold body. It can be feisty with its own kind and grows larger than many expect.
tips: Do not confuse with true Siamese algae eaters.
Keep one per tank.

items.name: Chinese Algae Eater
items.diet: Omnivore: algae, algae wafers, vegetables
items.note: Often sold as an algae eater, but it grows large and tends to become aggressive. Adults can also suck onto other fish.
tips: Not a good choice for community tanks as it ages.
Keep only one.

items.name: Medaka (Ricefish)
items.diet: Micro pellets, flakes
items.note: A tiny, hardy rice fish that does well in cool, unheated tanks. Many color varieties exist, all with the same care.
tips: Tolerates cool water.
Floating plants help with spawning.

items.name: Limia
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, vegetable foods
items.note: Livebearers related to mollies and guppies that like hard, alkaline water with plenty of plant matter in their diet.
tips: Prefers harder water.
Offer vegetable-based foods.

items.name: Julii Cory
items.diet: Sinking pellets, wafers, frozen foods
items.note: A spotted corydoras with a sweet nature. Keep in a group on soft sand or smooth gravel.
tips: Keep a group of four or more.
Use smooth substrate to protect barbels.
Often sold as julii or three-line cory.

items.name: Sterbai Cory
items.diet: Sinking pellets, wafers, frozen foods
items.note: A striking dotted cory with orange pectoral fins that tolerates warmer water than most corys. Good with discus and other warm-water fish.
tips: Keep a group of four or more.
Smooth sand protects its barbels.

items.name: Pygmy Cory
items.diet: Micro pellets, crushed wafers, frozen foods
items.note: A tiny corydoras that swims mid-water as well as along the bottom. Great for nano tanks in a group.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Feed tiny foods.

items.name: Skunk Cory
items.diet: Sinking pellets, wafers, frozen foods
items.note: A small cory marked with a dark stripe from nose to tail. Easy and active in a group.
tips: Keep a group of four or more.

items.name: Albino Cory
items.diet: Sinking pellets, wafers, frozen foods
items.note: A pale, pink-eyed form of the bronze cory. Same easy care; keep it in a group on smooth substrate.
tips: Keep a group of four or more.
Albino fish may dislike very bright light.

items.name: Assorted Corydoras
items.diet: Sinking pellets, wafers, frozen foods
items.note: Most corydoras share the same care: a group of four or more, smooth sand or gravel, and clean, stable water.
tips: Keep a group of four or more of one species.
Use smooth substrate.
Check the exact species for size and temperature.

items.name: Common Pleco
items.diet: Omnivore: algae wafers, vegetables, driftwood
items.note: Common plecos are sold small but grow to a foot or more and produce a lot of waste. Only get one if you can provide a large tank.
tips: Plan for a big tank (125 gallons or more).
Offer driftwood and vegetables.
It is not a cleanup crew.

items.name: Golden Nugget Pleco
items.diet: Omnivore: wafers, vegetables, frozen foods
items.note: A striking spotted pleco from the Xingu. Needs warm, well-oxygenated, clean water with caves and flow.
tips: Needs warm, oxygen-rich water.
Provide caves; do not overcrowd.
aka: l177 gold seam golden nugget pleco

items.name: Clown Pleco
items.diet: Wood-eater: driftwood, wafers, vegetables
items.note: A small, striped pleco that rasps on driftwood as part of its diet, so always provide wood. A good small-tank choice.
tips: Keep driftwood in the tank at all times.
Provide a cave.

items.name: Zebra Pleco
items.diet: Carnivore leaning omnivore: frozen foods, sinking pellets
items.note: A bold black-and-white pleco that needs warm, very clean, well-oxygenated water and caves. Prized and best for experienced keepers.
tips: Needs warm, clean, high-oxygen water.
Feed meaty frozen foods.
Provide small caves.

items.name: Royal Pleco
items.diet: Wood-eater: driftwood, vegetables, wafers
items.note: A large, handsome pleco that needs a lot of driftwood and a very large tank when grown.
tips: Provide plenty of driftwood.
Plan for a large tank.

items.name: Whiptail Catfish
items.diet: Algae, blanched vegetables, sinking foods
items.note: Slim, twig-like catfish that graze on algae and soft biofilm. Need clean, well-oxygenated water and gentle tankmates.
tips: Add only to mature tanks with biofilm.
Needs high-quality water.

items.name: Hoplo Catfish
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, frozen foods, worms
items.note: A hardy armored catfish that scavenges on the bottom and can eat very small fish.
tips: Provide caves.
Do not keep with tiny fish.

items.name: Synodontis Catfish
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, frozen foods, vegetables
items.note: A large group of African catfish that includes upside-down catfish, featherfin and petricola types. Size and temperament vary, so check the exact species.
tips: Provide caves.
Size varies a lot by species.

items.name: Pictus Catfish
items.diet: Carnivore leaning omnivore: pellets, frozen foods
items.note: An active, spotted catfish with long barbels. It will eat small tankmates and needs a long tank.
tips: Do not keep with tiny fish.
Needs swimming room.

items.name: Raphael Catfish
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A talking catfish that hides during the day and makes a squeaking sound. Provide hiding spots.
tips: Provide caves and hiding places.
Will eat very small fish.

items.name: Banjo Catfish
items.diet: Sinking foods, frozen worms
items.note: A flat, leaf-like catfish that buries itself in sand. Needs a soft sandy bottom and gentle tankmates.
tips: Use soft sand.
Feed after lights out.

items.name: Yoyo Loach
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, frozen foods, snails
items.note: An active, playful loach with a pattern that resembles the letters of its name when young. Best in a group.
tips: Keep a group of five or more.
Provide caves.

items.name: Dojo Loach
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets, frozen foods, worms
items.note: A hardy, eel-like loach that tolerates cooler water. Needs soft sand and a tight lid because it can escape.
tips: Use soft sand.
Use a tight lid.
Reacts to pressure changes.

items.name: Zebra Loach
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking foods, frozen foods
items.note: A small, striped loach that is active and social. Keep with a group and provide caves.
tips: Keep three or more.
Provide caves.

items.name: Hillstream Loach
items.diet: Algae and biofilm, small frozen foods
items.note: A flat, fast-water loach that grazes on algae and biofilm. Needs cool, highly oxygenated, flowing water.
tips: Needs cool, oxygen-rich, flowing water.
Add to a mature tank with biofilm.

items.name: Botia Loach
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking foods, frozen foods
items.note: Botia loaches are active, social bottom fish. Several species are sold; check the exact one for adult size.
tips: Keep in groups.
Provide caves.

items.name: Dwarf Chain Loach
items.diet: Omnivore: small sinking foods, frozen foods
items.note: A tiny, busy loach that does best in a group. Needs stable, clean water and caves.
tips: Keep six or more.
Feed small foods.

items.name: Horseface Loach
items.diet: Sinking foods, worms
items.note: A sand-sifting loach that buries itself and sifts the substrate. Needs soft sand.
tips: Needs fine soft sand.
Gentle tankmates only.

items.name: Giant Gourami
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, vegetables, frozen foods
items.note: Small giant gouramis are sold young, but they grow to two feet and need a pond-size aquarium.
tips: Only for very large tanks.
Plan for decades of care.

items.name: Opaline Gourami
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A hardy, larger gourami with a marbled pattern. Males can become territorial with each other.
tips: Keep one male per tank.
Provide floating plants.

items.name: Flame Gourami
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: The red-orange form of the dwarf gourami group. Peaceful and easy in a planted community tank.
tips: Provide floating plants.
Keep one male per tank.
Same species as the dwarf gourami: buy from clean tanks, quarantine, and watch for disease.

items.name: Licorice Gourami
items.diet: Tiny live and frozen foods
items.note: A tiny, delicate blackwater gourami that needs soft, acidic water and live foods. For experienced keepers.
tips: Needs soft, acidic water.
Feed tiny live or frozen foods.

items.name: Paradise Fish
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A hardy, colorful labyrinth fish that tolerates cool water but is aggressive toward its own kind and small tankmates.
tips: Keep one male per tank.
Use a lid with a gap for air.

items.name: Plakat Betta
items.diet: Carnivore leaning omnivore: betta pellets, frozen foods
items.note: Plakat bettas are short-finned varieties, active and hardy. Keep males singly, and pair only with calm tankmates.
tips: One male per tank.
Heated, filtered tanks only.

items.name: Severum
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, vegetables, frozen foods
items.note: A large, deep-bodied cichlid that is generally calmer than other big cichlids. Does best in a roomy tank with steady water changes.
tips: Needs a large tank.
Offer vegetables as part of the diet.

items.name: Peacock Bass
items.diet: Carnivore: whole foods, frozen fish, shrimp
items.note: A fast, predatory cichlid that grows large and needs a very large tank and strong filtration. Not for casual keepers.
tips: Needs a very large tank; the largest species need far more than 300 gallons.
Eats fish.

items.name: Geophagus
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets, frozen foods
items.note: Sand-sifting eartheaters that sift through the substrate. Need fine sand and open space.
tips: Use fine sand.
Do regular water changes.

items.name: Blood Parrot Cichlid
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A captive-bred hybrid with a rounded head and small mouth. Hardy but can be territorial.
tips: Needs a roomy tank.
Dye-enhanced fish may lose color.

items.name: Firemouth Cichlid
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A hardy Central American cichlid that flares its red throat when threatened.
tips: Needs a roomy tank.
Provide caves.

items.name: Tropheus
items.diet: Algae and vegetable foods; avoid high protein
items.note: A rock-dwelling cichlid from Lake Tanganyika that lives in large groups. It needs hard, alkaline water and a vegetable-based diet.
tips: Needs hard, alkaline water.
Use a plant-based diet; high protein can cause bloat.

items.name: Multifasciatus Shell Dweller
items.diet: Small frozen and live foods, micro pellets
items.note: A tiny cichlid that lives and breeds in empty snail shells. Great for a colony tank with a sand bottom.
tips: Use sand and plenty of empty shells.
Needs hard, alkaline water.

items.name: Uaru
items.diet: Omnivore: vegetables, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A shy, large, disc-shaped cichlid that needs soft, clean water and a roomy tank.
tips: Needs soft, very clean water.
Keep calm tankmates.

items.name: German Gold Ram
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A golden form of the ram cichlid. Needs warm, clean water and stable conditions.
tips: Keep warm and stable.
Feed small foods.

items.name: Apistogramma
items.diet: Carnivore leaning omnivore: frozen foods, micro pellets
items.note: Dwarf cichlids with big personalities. Males are larger and more colorful. Provide caves and plants.
tips: Provide caves.
Keep one male with several females.

items.name: Electric Blue Jack Dempsey
items.diet: Carnivore leaning omnivore: pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A vivid blue cultivated form of the Jack Dempsey. Territorial and not suited to small or peaceful tankmates.
tips: Needs a large tank.
Keep with similarly sized fish.

items.name: Green Spotted Puffer
items.diet: Carnivore: snails, shrimp, crustaceans
items.note: A bold, intelligent puffer that grows up in brackish water. It needs hard-shelled foods to keep its teeth worn down and eats most tankmates.
tips: Brackish long term: juveniles can start in low salinity, but adults need brackish to near-marine water, so plan for a saltwater test kit.
Feed snails and shelled foods.
Keep alone.

items.name: Fahaka Puffer
items.diet: Carnivore: snails, shrimp, crustaceans
items.note: A large, aggressive freshwater puffer that needs a very large tank and a diet of hard-shelled foods.
tips: Keep alone.
Feed hard-shelled foods for its teeth.
Needs a very large tank.

items.name: Mbu Puffer
items.diet: Carnivore: snails, shrimp, crustaceans
items.note: The largest freshwater puffer, needing an enormous tank. For specialists only.
tips: Needs a very large tank.
Keep alone.

items.name: Specialty Puffers
items.diet: Carnivore: snails, shrimp, crustaceans
items.note: Pufferfish vary a lot in size and temperament, but most eat hard-shelled foods and nip fins. Check the exact species before buying: some, such as the orange saddle (fugu) types, may need brackish water as adults, and the Congo and Amazon puffers can reach 5-6 in and a bigger tank than this entry's minimum.
tips: Research each species.
Feed hard-shelled foods.
Most should be kept alone.

items.name: Bichir
items.diet: Carnivore: pellets, frozen foods
items.note: Ancient-looking, long-lived fish that can breathe air. Many species grow to a foot or more. Use a tight lid because they escape.
tips: Use a tight lid.
Do not keep with small fish.

items.name: Knifefish
items.diet: Carnivore: frozen foods, pellets
items.note: Long, flattened fish that hunt at night. Many grow large and eat small tankmates; the clown knifefish alone reaches about three feet and needs a tank sized for that, not for the juvenile sold in stores.
tips: Plan for a tank of 250 gallons or more for an adult clown knifefish.
Provide hiding spots.
Do not keep with small fish.

items.name: Elephantnose Fish
items.diet: Carnivore: live and frozen blackworms, bloodworms
items.note: A fascinating, nocturnal electric fish that senses its world through an electric field. Needs soft sand, hiding spots, and calm tankmates.
tips: Use soft sand.
Offer worms; it is often a picky eater.

items.name: Silver Dollar
items.diet: Herbivore leaning omnivore: vegetables, pellets, flakes
items.note: A disc-shaped schooling fish that eats plants and needs a roomy, long tank.
tips: Keep a group of five or more.
Offer vegetables; it eats soft plants.

items.name: Red Belly Pacu
items.diet: Omnivore: vegetables, fruit, pellets
items.note: Pacu are sold small but grow large and fast, with some individuals reaching close to three feet, and need a tank measured in the hundreds of gallons, not a standard community tank.
tips: Not suitable for most homes.
Needs a huge tank, several hundred gallons or more for a full-grown fish.

items.name: Datnoid
items.diet: Carnivore: frozen fish, shrimp, live foods
items.note: A striking striped predator that needs a large tank and meaty foods. Sold small, it reaches well over a foot and should be given a tank at least six feet long.
tips: Do not keep with small fish.
Needs a large tank.

items.name: Gar
items.diet: Carnivore: whole fish
items.note: Long, ambush predators that need very large tanks and secure lids. Specialist fish. Spotted and Florida gar stay near 2-3 ft, while longnose and alligator gar grow much larger (alligator gar reach 6 ft or more and suit ponds only, and are not recommended here). Fish sold as hujeta gar or freshwater barracuda are South American pike characins, which stay smaller but still need a long, covered tank.
tips: Needs a very large tank.
Use a heavy lid.

items.name: Black Arowana and Other Arowana
items.diet: Carnivore: insects, fish, shrimp
items.note: Arowana grow very large and need huge, long tanks with secure lids. Several species are sold; check legal and care requirements.
tips: Needs a very large tank and tight lid.
Check species and legal requirements.

items.name: Koi
items.diet: Omnivore: koi pellets, vegetables
items.note: Koi are pond fish that grow very large. Small koi can live in aquariums only temporarily.
tips: Plan for a pond.
Cannot stay in small tanks.
aka: koi fish assorted bundle of three

items.name: Killifish
items.diet: Small live and frozen foods, micro pellets
items.note: Often brightly colored, jump-prone fish that sit near the surface. Many are short-lived. Use a tight lid.
tips: Use a tight lid.
Offer live or frozen foods.

items.name: Rainbowfish
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: Active, colorful schooling fish that need long tanks and hard, alkaline water.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Give it room to swim.
Prefers harder water.

items.name: Pencilfish
items.diet: Micro pellets, frozen foods, baby brine shrimp
items.note: Slender, shy fish with a bold stripe, best in a planted tank with dim light.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Use a tight lid.

items.name: Assassin Snail
items.diet: Carnivore: snails, frozen foods
items.note: A striped snail that hunts other snails. Useful against pest snails, but it will also eat ramshorns, mystery snails and sometimes nerites. It breeds slowly, so a few are enough.
tips: Do not keep with snails you want to keep.
Feed meaty foods if snails run out.

items.name: Ramshorn Snail
items.diet: Algae, detritus, vegetables
items.note: Flat, coil-shelled snails that reproduce quickly and eat algae and leftover food.
tips: Population follows food supply.
Safe with most plants.

items.name: Trapdoor Snail
items.diet: Algae, detritus
items.note: A live-bearing snail with a sealable operculum. Prefers cooler water.
tips: Prefers cool to moderate temperatures.
Does not eat plants.

items.name: Rabbit Snail
items.diet: Algae, detritus, sinking foods, vegetables
items.note: A large, cone-shaped Sulawesi snail that produces only a few young at a time. Likes warm, hard, alkaline water.
tips: Needs warm, hard water.
Safe with plants.

items.name: Inca Snail
items.diet: Algae, detritus, sinking foods
items.note: A hardy snail that burrows in sand and grazes.
tips: Safe with plants.
Burrows in sand.

items.name: Bamboo Shrimp
items.diet: Filter feeder: powdered foods, fine particles
items.note: A filter-feeding shrimp that fans its arms in the current. Needs a mature tank with fine food particles.
tips: Use a gentle flow.
Feed powdered foods.

items.name: Caridina Shrimp
items.diet: Algae, biofilm, shrimp foods
items.note: Crystal, bee and tiger shrimp often need softer, more stable water than neocaridina. Use RO water remineralized for shrimp.
tips: Use stable, soft water.
Avoid copper and sudden changes.

items.name: Neocaridina Color Shrimp
items.diet: Algae, biofilm, shrimp foods
items.note: Easy shrimp in many colors: yellow, blue, green, black, orange, and rili patterns. Same care as cherry shrimp.
tips: Keep a group.
Avoid copper.

items.name: Dwarf and Specialty Crayfish
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets, vegetables, frozen foods
items.note: Crayfish are escape artists and will eat small fish and shrimp. Dwarf Mexican crayfish stay smaller and are gentler.
tips: Use a tight lid.
Provide hiding spots.
Do not keep with shrimp or small fish.

items.name: Freshwater Crab
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, vegetables, frozen foods
items.note: Vampire, panda, red devil and other crabs are semi-terrestrial. They need land area and a very secure lid.
tips: Provide land and water.
Use a very secure lid.

items.name: Dwarf Hermit Crab
items.diet: Algae, detritus, sinking foods
items.note: Often sold as freshwater hermit crabs, but these are saltwater animals and cannot live long term in freshwater. We mention it so you can choose accurately.
tips: Not a true freshwater animal.
Ask staff for suitable freshwater alternatives.

items.name: Freshwater Clam
items.diet: Filter feeder: fine particles, algae
items.note: Filter-feeding clams are difficult to feed well in home tanks and often starve. Only for experienced keepers.
tips: Need an established tank with microscopic food.
Often short-lived.

items.name: Black Neon Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: A small, hardy tetra with a white-edged black body stripe. It is a different species from the common neon tetra, with its own look and slightly different water preferences, and it does well in a planted community tank.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Not a neon tetra; do not rely on neon care notes for exact numbers.
Choose calm, small tankmates.

items.name: Green Neon Tetra
items.origin: Rio Negro and Orinoco basins, South America
items.diet: Micro pellets, crushed flakes, baby brine shrimp, small frozen foods
items.note: A tiny cousin of the neon tetra with a bright green-blue stripe and no red on the body. It is smaller and shyer than a neon and prefers softer, clean, stable water in a quiet planted tank.
tips: Keep a group of eight or more.
Only pair with small, gentle tankmates.
Make changes to the water slowly.

items.name: Redtail Catfish
items.origin: Amazon and Orinoco basins, South America
items.temperament: Predatory, will eat anything that fits
items.diet: Carnivore: fish, shrimp, squid, large sinking pellets
items.note: Sold as a cute juvenile, the redtail catfish grows into a heavy, powerful fish about three to four feet long. It needs a tank measured in the high hundreds or thousands of gallons, which is why it is usually a fish for a public aquarium or a pond-sized setup.
tips: Plan for a tank of 1,000 gallons or more before buying.
Do not keep with any fish small enough to swallow.
Use heavy equipment covers and strong filtration.

items.name: Ghost Shrimp
items.temperament: Peaceful, but may eat tiny shrimp and fry
items.diet: Omnivore: algae wafers, sinking pellets, leftover food, biofilm
items.note: A see-through freshwater shrimp that cleans up scraps and is fun to watch. It lives only about a year or two, and it is larger and more predatory than cherry shrimp, so do not count on baby shrimp surviving in the same tank.
tips: Avoid copper-based medications.
Provide hiding spots for molting.
Do not mix with tiny shrimp you want to breed.

items.name: Emerald Catfish
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets and wafers, frozen foods
items.note: A shimmering green armored catfish that is taller and longer than most corydoras. Keep a group on soft sand or smooth gravel and feed foods that sink.
tips: Keep five or more together.
Use smooth sand or fine gravel.
Needs a larger tank than small corydoras.

items.name: Dwarf Neon Rainbowfish
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: A small, bright rainbowfish with a blue body and red fins. It is a good fit for medium community tanks, needs a group and open swimming space, and does best in clean, moderately hard water.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Use a tight lid; rainbowfish jump.
Feed small portions, twice a day.

items.name: Blue Acara
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, frozen foods, vegetables
items.note: A hardy, medium-sized cichlid with blue-green markings. It is calmer than most large cichlids but will eat small fish and defend a territory when breeding.
tips: Do not keep with small fish like neons.
Provide caves and open swimming space.
Use a sturdy lid and strong filtration.

items.name: Keyhole Cichlid
items.diet: Omnivore: small pellets, frozen foods, live foods
items.note: A calm, shy cichlid named for the keyhole-shaped dark mark on its side. It does best in a quiet tank with plants, caves and gentle tankmates.
tips: Use calm tankmates; boisterous fish stress it.
Provide caves and plants.
Keep water clean and stable.

items.name: Sparkling Gourami
items.diet: Carnivore: micro pellets, baby brine shrimp, small frozen foods
items.note: A tiny labyrinth fish with iridescent dots and the ability to make soft croaking sounds. It needs a calm, planted tank with floating plants and very gentle tankmates.
tips: Leave an air gap under the lid.
Use floating plants for cover.
Feed tiny live or frozen foods.

items.name: Pearl Danio
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A fast, hardy schooling danio with a pearly sheen and a hint of pink or blue. It needs a long tank with open water and a secure lid.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Use a tight lid; danios jump.
Choose a tank that is at least two feet long.

items.name: Red Eye Tetra
items.temperament: Active, mostly peaceful, may nip long fins
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A silver tetra with a red ring above the eye. Hardy and active, it likes to be in a group and may nibble the fins of long-finned fish.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Avoid long-finned tankmates.
Tough plants work best; it can nibble soft ones.

items.name: Checker Barb
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A small, peaceful barb with a checkered scale pattern and orange-tinged fins on the males. It is hardy, likes cooler water than many tropical fish, and is a calm pick for community tanks.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Tolerates cooler tropical temperatures.
Use a lid; barbs can jump.

items.name: Columbian Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A sturdy tetra with a blue-violet sheen and a reddish tail. It is more active than neon-type tetras and can nibble long fins, so pair it with fast, similar-sized fish.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Avoid bettas and other long-finned fish.
Give it open swimming room.

items.name: Rosy Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A peaceful tetra with a rosy body and a black-and-white edged dorsal fin on males. Good for a planted community tank; the long-finned variety is more delicate.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Choose calm tankmates.
Keep water clean and stable.

items.name: Ruby Tetra
items.diet: Micro pellets, crushed flakes, baby brine shrimp
items.note: A tiny, shy tetra with a red-orange shimmer. It is best in a calm planted tank with soft, clean water and only very small, gentle tankmates.
tips: Keep eight or more.
Do not mix with boisterous fish.
Add only to a mature tank.

items.name: Gold Tetra
items.origin: Guyana and nearby northern South America
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A hardy tetra with gold-glinting scales. It is calm and a good choice for beginners with a community tank.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Tolerates a range of water.
Use gentle filtration.

items.name: Glowlight Danio
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, small frozen foods
items.note: A small, peaceful danio with a glowing orange stripe. It suits a small community tank and needs a lid, since danios jump.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Use a tight lid.
Feed small foods.

items.name: Five-Banded Barb
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: A small barb with bold dark bands. It is shy, likes soft, slightly acidic water and a planted tank with calm tankmates; often kept in a larger group to look its best.
tips: Keep eight or more.
Do not mix with fast, boisterous fish.
Plants and wood help it feel secure.

items.name: Glass Catfish
items.diet: Small live, frozen or sinking foods; some fish accept micro pellets
items.note: A transparent catfish that swims in mid-water and needs a group. It is shy and sensitive to poor water, so do not mix it with bullies or fast feeders.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Avoid strong flow and boisterous tankmates.
Do not dye-treat or paint-dye fish; buy natural fish.

items.name: Upside-Down Catfish
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets, frozen foods, algae
items.note: A small synodontis that often swims upside down at the surface or under plants and wood. It is peaceful, nocturnal and happiest with caves and a group.
tips: Provide caves and wood.
Keep at least three if the tank allows.
Do not mix with tiny shrimp.

items.name: Bumblebee Catfish
items.temperament: Predatory toward tiny fish and shrimp
items.diet: Carnivore: frozen foods, live foods, sinking pellets
items.note: A small, boldly banded catfish that hides by day. It will eat fish and shrimp that fit in its mouth, so keep it with fish bigger than about an inch and a half.
tips: Provide caves and cover.
Do not keep with neons or small shrimp.
Feed sinking foods in the evening.

items.name: Festivum Cichlid
items.origin: Amazon and Orinoco basins, South America
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: A tall, flat-bodied cichlid with a dark flank stripe. It is calmer than many cichlids but can be territorial when breeding and may eat very small fish.
tips: Provide height, caves and wood.
Do not keep with tiny tetras.
Use a larger tank for a group.

items.name: Green Terror
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, frozen foods, vegetables
items.note: A bold, blue-green cichlid with a bright face. Males grow big and aggressive and are best in a large tank with sturdy tankmates of similar size.
tips: Plan for a large tank for an adult.
Provide caves and broken sight lines.
Do not keep with small fish.

items.name: Sailfin Pleco
items.temperament: Peaceful, may become territorial with other plecos
items.diet: Herbivore: algae wafers, vegetables, driftwood, some protein
items.note: A spotted pleco with a tall sail-like dorsal fin. It grows far larger than the juveniles sold, needs a very large tank and produces a lot of waste. Never release it into local waters.
tips: Plan on a large tank for an adult.
Provide driftwood and hiding places.
Do not release plecos outdoors.

items.name: Rubber Lip Pleco
items.diet: Herbivore: algae wafers, blanched vegetables, biofilm
items.note: A mid-sized, grey-spotted pleco from flowing water. It likes cooler tropical temperatures, strong oxygen and driftwood to rasp on.
tips: Use good filtration and oxygenation.
Provide driftwood and rock.
Feed vegetables as well as wafers.

items.name: Kissing Gourami
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, algae, vegetables
items.note: A large gourami known for its lip-to-lip pushing, which is usually a contest, not affection. It grows bigger than most store fish suggest and eats a lot of plant matter.
tips: Plan for a large tank.
Expect plants to be nibbled.
Leave an air gap under the lid.

items.name: Chocolate Gourami
items.diet: Small live and frozen foods; many refuse dry food
items.note: A delicate, shy gourami that wants soft, acidic, spotless water and calm tankmates. It is not a beginner fish and is easily stressed by moves and poor water.
tips: Use only a mature, stable tank.
Offer small live or frozen foods.
Do not mix with active fish.

items.name: Peppered Cory
items.diet: Sinking pellets and wafers, frozen and live worms
items.note: One of the oldest and hardiest corydoras in the hobby, with a speckled olive body. It tolerates cooler water than most corys, so it suits unheated rooms and mixes with goldfish-range temperatures better than tropical-only species.
tips: Keep a group of five or more on smooth sand or fine gravel.
Feed sinking foods after lights-out if tankmates are quick.
Sharp gravel damages the barbels and leads to infections.

items.name: Iridescent Shark
items.origin: Mekong and Chao Phraya basins, Southeast Asia
items.temperament: Peaceful but panicky, grows too big for tankmates
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets, frozen foods, vegetables
items.note: Sold as a sleek silver juvenile, this catfish is not a true shark and grows into a large, heavy fish. It is skittish and often injures itself in glass, so it is a poor fit for home aquariums and is best left to pond-scale or public setups.
tips: Plan for a tank measured in the hundreds to thousands of gallons before buying.
Juveniles dart into glass when startled; keep the room calm.
Do not buy it as a community fish for a standard tank.

items.name: Jewel Cichlid
items.diet: Carnivore leaning omnivore: pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A small African cichlid with deep red-to-jewel coloring that bullies tankmates when it breeds. Stores often sell several look-alike Hemichromis species under one name, so adult size and temperament vary a little.
tips: Give it its own tank or choose large, sturdy tankmates.
Provide caves; a pair claims a large territory when spawning.
Expect to separate a pair from other fish during breeding.

items.name: Midas Cichlid
items.social: Single or pair with plenty of space
items.diet: Carnivore leaning omnivore: cichlid pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A big, intelligent Central American cichlid, often sold as the red devil cichlid. It digs, rearranges decor and defends its territory, so it needs a large tank and strong filtration.
tips: Plan for a 150-gallon tank or larger for one adult.
Secure heavy decor and heaters; it will move and break them.
Do large water changes often.

items.name: Peacock Cichlid
items.social: Group with one male and several females
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A colorful Malawi sand-dweller; males show blue, red or yellow while females stay drab. They are calmer than mbuna and do best with similar mild species in hard, alkaline water.
tips: Keep one male with several females to share the chasing.
Use hard, alkaline water and a sand substrate.
Do not mix with aggressive rock-dwelling mbuna.

items.name: Frontosa Cichlid
items.temperament: Calm but a large predator of small fish
items.diet: Carnivore: large pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A slow, stately Tanganyika cichlid with bold black bars and a pronounced forehead on males. It is long-lived and sensitive to poor water, so it suits experienced keepers with large tanks and very hard, alkaline water.
tips: Plan for 125 gallons for one or two fish and 180 or more for a group.
Keep water hard, alkaline and very clean.
Avoid overfeeding; digestive problems are common.

items.name: Julidochromis
items.diet: Omnivore: small cichlid pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A small, torpedo-shaped Tanganyika cichlid that lives among rocks and crevices. Pairs are devoted but chase other fish out of their cave area.
tips: Stack rocks to make many caves and crevices.
Use hard, alkaline water.
Add one pair, not a group, to a small tank.
J. regani and J. marlieri grow larger (5-6 in) and want a 55-gallon or bigger tank.

items.name: Daffodil Cichlid
items.diet: Omnivore: small pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A graceful, long-finned Tanganyika cichlid known as the princess of Burundi. It lives in family groups where older young help guard fry, so it is fun to watch in a rocky tank.
tips: Start with one pair or a few and let the group grow.
Build caves from stacked rock.
Use hard, alkaline water.

items.name: Moonlight Gourami
items.origin: Mekong and Chao Phraya basins, Southeast Asia
items.social: Single, pair or small group in a big tank
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A calm, silvery gourami with thread-like pelvic fins that shimmer under dim light. It is shy at first and likes floating plants and warm, stable water.
tips: Use a lid with an air gap.
Add floating plants to help it settle.
Avoid very active fin-nippers.

items.name: Malaysian Trumpet Snail
items.diet: Detritus, leftover food, algae
items.note: A cone-shaped burrowing snail that stirs sand, eats leftover food and keeps substrate from packing. It breeds quickly when feeding is heavy, so numbers show how much food the tank gets.
tips: Do not overfeed; a population boom means excess food.
Use it as an indicator of waste, not a cleanup crew.
Prefer harder, alkaline water.

items.name: Rope Fish (Reedfish)
items.temperament: Peaceful with large fish, eats small ones
items.diet: Carnivore: sinking pellets, frozen and live worms, shrimp pieces
items.note: A long, eel-like fish from Africa that breathes air at the surface and hunts mostly at night. It is calm with fish too big to swallow but will eat anything that fits in its mouth, and it is a skilled escape artist.
tips: Cover every gap in the lid; it will find them.
Do not keep with small fish like neons or with shrimp.
Feed sinking foods, since it finds food by smell and touch.

items.name: Exclamation Point Rasbora
items.diet: Micro pellets, crushed flakes, baby brine shrimp, tiny frozen foods
items.note: One of the smallest aquarium fish, named for the dark stripe and spot that look like an exclamation point. It needs a calm planted tank, a group, and tankmates small and gentle enough not to bully or eat it.
tips: Keep a group of eight or more.
Only pair with very small, calm tankmates.
Feed tiny foods and keep the tank clean and stable.

items.name: Pretty Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, small frozen foods
items.note: A small, peaceful tetra with a silvery body and a dark patch near the tail. It does best in a group, in a tank with plants and subdued light.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Add to a fully cycled, stable tank.
Choose calm tankmates of similar size.

items.name: Royal Tetra (Blue Emperor Tetra)
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, small frozen foods
items.note: A small tetra with a blue sheen and a yellow-edged tail. It is peaceful and sturdy, and shows its best color in a group in a planted tank with darker substrate.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
A dark substrate and plants bring out the blue.
Not the same fish as the black emperor tetra.

items.name: Golden Dwarf Danio (Gold Ring Danio)
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, crushed flakes, baby brine shrimp
items.note: A tiny, glittering danio with a golden sheen and dark bars on the body. It is active, does best in a group, and likes a lid because it can jump.
tips: Keep a group of eight or more.
Use a tight lid.
Choose tiny, peaceful tankmates.

items.name: Thick-Lipped Gourami
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, small pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A calm, colorful gourami closely related to the honey gourami but a bit larger. It suits a planted community tank and tolerates a fairly wide range of water.
tips: Leave an air gap under the lid.
Keep only one male unless the tank is large and planted.
Use floating plants for cover.

items.name: Frogmouth Catfish
items.temperament: Ambush predator, eats any fish it can swallow
items.diet: Carnivore: frozen or live fish and shrimp, worms, sinking carnivore pellets
items.note: A camouflaged ambush hunter that sits motionless on the bottom, looking like a decaying leaf, and lunges at anything small enough to swallow. It is a fascinating but specialist fish that needs a tank with no small tankmates.
tips: Do not keep with small fish or shrimp.
Provide soft sand, leaf litter and wood to rest on.
It is mostly active at night; feed in the evening.

items.name: Six-Barred Distichodus
items.temperament: Semi-aggressive, territorial with its own kind
items.diet: Mostly herbivore: spirulina pellets, blanched greens, some frozen foods
items.note: A boldly striped African fish that is sold small but reaches well over a foot. It eats most live plants and can bully smaller tankmates, so it fits large tanks with fish of similar size.
tips: Plan on a very large tank before buying.
It eats most live plants; use tough plants or none.
Offer greens and vegetable-based foods daily.

items.name: Pike Cichlid
items.diet: Carnivore: fish and shrimp pieces, large pellets, earthworms
items.note: Long, slender predatory cichlids that hide in caves and wood and ambush small fish. Adult size varies by species, so confirm the exact fish and plan for a cave-rich tank with sturdy tankmates only.
tips: Do not keep with fish small enough to swallow.
Provide caves, wood and a secure lid.
Ask which species you are buying; some stay near 8 in and some reach over a foot.

items.name: Panda Garra
items.diet: Omnivore: algae wafers, sinking pellets, blanched vegetables, small frozen foods
items.note: A small, black-and-white algae grazer that sucks onto rocks and wood. It likes clean, well-oxygenated water with moderate flow and plenty of surfaces to graze.
tips: Provide flow and good filtration.
Keep a small group so they feel secure.
Offer algae-based foods as well as meaty foods.

items.name: Snowball Pleco (L201)
items.diet: Omnivore leaning carnivore: sinking pellets, frozen bloodworms, brine shrimp, some vegetables
items.note: A small, white-spotted pleco that stays compact and lives in caves. It likes warm, clean, well-oxygenated water, so it suits an established tank rather than a first aquarium.
tips: Provide several caves, one per fish.
Keep water warm, clean and well oxygenated.
Feed meaty sinking foods; do not rely on algae alone.

items.name: Red Terror Cichlid
items.origin: Pacific slope of Ecuador and Peru
items.social: Solitary or a bonded pair in a very large tank
items.diet: Carnivore leaning omnivore: cichlid pellets, frozen foods, earthworms
items.note: A big, bold Central and South American cichlid with a blue-green body and a red-orange flush. It is strong, digs, and can be fierce toward tankmates, so it is a one-fish centerpiece for a very large tank.
tips: Plan for 150 gallons or more for one adult.
Keep only with similar large, tough fish, if at all.
Use heavy decor and secure equipment; it digs and moves things.

items.name: Threadfin Acara
items.origin: Amazon and Guianas, northern South America
items.diet: Omnivore leaning carnivore: pellets, frozen foods, worms
items.note: A sand-sifting South American cichlid with a mottled pattern and a dark spot on the side. It is calmer than many large cichlids but still needs a roomy tank and fish of similar size.
tips: Use soft sand so it can sift without scratching its mouth.
Keep tankmates too big to swallow and not easily bullied.
Provide caves or wood for pairs that breed.

items.name: Green Phantom Pleco
items.origin: Northern South America (sold under trade code L200)
items.social: Solitary or small groups in big tanks
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets, vegetables, frozen foods, driftwood to rasp
items.note: A dark-green pleco with pale spots, known by the trade code L200. It stays smaller than a common pleco but likes warm, oxygen-rich water, caves, and wood to graze on.
tips: Provide caves and driftwood.
Keep the water warm, clean and well oxygenated.
Do not mix it up with larger common plecos; check the exact fish.

items.name: Head and Tail Light Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, small frozen foods
items.note: A small, silvery tetra with glowing spots near the eye and the base of the tail, also called the beacon fish. It is hardy and peaceful and does well in a planted community tank.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Choose small, calm tankmates.
Feed small foods that fit its mouth.

items.name: Glowlight Rasbora
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, baby brine shrimp
items.note: A tiny, peaceful rasbora with a glowing orange stripe along the body. Keep a group in a planted tank with calm tankmates and stable water.
tips: Keep eight or more together.
Choose gentle tankmates of similar size.
Avoid rapid water changes in temperature and hardness.

items.name: Salt and Pepper Cory
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking micro pellets, wafers, frozen foods
items.note: A tiny, peppery-patterned corydoras that stays small and likes soft sand. Keep a group at the bottom of a peaceful tank, and feed foods that sink within its reach.
tips: Use smooth sand or fine gravel.
Keep six or more.
Do not mix with fish large enough to eat it.

items.name: Vampire Shrimp
items.diet: Filter feeder: fine powdered foods, floating particles, biofilm
items.note: A large, peaceful filter-feeding shrimp that uses fan-like hands to catch particles from the water. It hides a lot and is shy after molting, so it needs a mature tank with strong flow, caves, and tankmates that will not pick on it.
tips: Add only to a mature tank with plenty of fine food in the water.
Provide caves and rocks to hide in.
Keep the lid on and avoid copper-based medications.

items.name: Red-Eye Puffer
items.social: Solitary or a well-planted group with experience
items.diet: Carnivore: snails, frozen bloodworms, brine shrimp, small live foods
items.note: A small freshwater puffer with a red eye, sold as a cousin of the dwarf puffer. It is curious but nips fins and may bully tankmates, so most keepers give it its own heavily planted tank and feed hard-shelled snails to wear down its teeth.
tips: Do not assume it is a community fish; it nips fins.
Offer snails regularly so its teeth stay worn down.
Keep the water very clean; puffers are messy eaters.

items.name: Clown Killifish
items.social: Small group, 1 male with a few females
items.diet: Carnivore: micro pellets, baby brine shrimp, daphnia, small frozen foods
items.note: A tiny banded killifish that spends its time near the surface. It is peaceful but short-lived and a skilled jumper, so it needs a tight lid, floating plants and very gentle tankmates.
tips: Use a tight lid; it jumps.
Add floating plants for cover.
Feed small live or frozen foods; many refuse dry food at first.

items.name: African Banded Barb
items.origin: Angola and the upper Congo and Zambezi basins, Africa
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: A small barb with several dark vertical bands on a golden body. It is peaceful and active and is best kept as a group in a planted tank with calm tankmates.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Use a tight lid; barbs can jump.
Keep the water clean and well filtered.

items.name: Black Ghost Knifefish
items.origin: Amazon and Paraguay basins, South America
items.temperament: Peaceful with large fish, eats small fish
items.diet: Carnivore: frozen bloodworms, mysis, krill, earthworms, sinking meaty pellets
items.note: A velvety black, nocturnal knifefish that swims forwards and backwards using a long ribbon fin. It is sold small but grows over a foot long, hides all day, and is sensitive to salt, strong medications and poor water.
tips: Provide hiding places like pipes and caves.
Do not keep with fish small enough to eat.
Avoid copper and use fish medications with extra care.

items.name: Auratus Cichlid
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, flakes, spirulina, vegetables
items.note: A striped Malawi mbuna. Young fish and females are gold with dark stripes while mature males turn mostly black with a blue sheen. It is feisty and territorial, so plan a rocky tank with plenty of hiding places and a group with more females than males.
tips: Keep one male with several females.
Stack rock to break lines of sight.
Use hard, alkaline water and avoid very small tankmates.

items.name: Johanni Cichlid
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, flakes, spirulina, vegetables
items.note: A Malawi mbuna with a striking sexual difference: females and young are orange-gold with dark stripes while mature males turn dark blue-black. It is territorial, so keep it in a rocky tank with several females per male and tough tankmates.
tips: Keep one male with several females.
Do not mix with other similar striped mbuna, since males fight.
Offer vegetable matter along with pellets.

items.name: Yellow-Tail Acei Cichlid
items.temperament: Mostly peaceful for a Malawi cichlid, some chasing
items.social: Group of 6+ in a large tank
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, spirulina, frozen foods
items.note: A slim, silvery-blue Malawi cichlid with a yellow tail. It is one of the calmer Malawi species but still needs rockwork, hard alkaline water and a group larger than a few fish to spread out any aggression.
tips: Keep a group in a long tank.
Use rock caves and open swimming room.
Use hard, alkaline water.

items.name: Electric Blue Hap
items.diet: Carnivore-leaning omnivore: cichlid pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A bright blue peacock-relative from Lake Malawi, often sold as electric blue ahli. It is a fish-eater at heart, so avoid very small tankmates and give it a long tank with open water and some rock.
tips: Do not keep with fish small enough to swallow.
Keep one male per tank unless the tank is large.
Use hard, alkaline water.

items.name: Snakeskin Gourami
items.temperament: Peaceful but large, can bully small fish
items.social: Solitary or pair in a very large tank
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, flakes, frozen foods, vegetables
items.note: A big, calm gourami with a snake-like pattern on its sides. Store fish are small, but adults reach about ten inches, so it belongs in a large, long tank with a lid that leaves an air gap.
tips: Plan for a tank of 75 gallons or more.
Leave an air gap above the water.
Avoid very small tankmates.

items.name: Bandit Cory
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets and wafers, frozen foods
items.note: A small armored catfish named for the dark mask across its eyes. Like other corydoras it is happiest in a group on soft sand or smooth gravel, and it adds lively activity at the bottom of a community tank.
tips: Keep five or more together.
Use sand or smooth gravel to protect its barbels.
Feed sinking foods so it is not outcompeted.

items.name: Black Ruby Barb
items.temperament: Peaceful to lively; may nip long fins
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods, some vegetables
items.note: A small, active barb whose males turn deep ruby and black when settled and well fed. It is hardy and good in community tanks, but keep a group so the nipping is spread out, and avoid slow, long-finned tankmates.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Avoid long-finned, slow tankmates.
Give it plants and some open swimming space.

items.name: Cobalt Blue Zebra Cichlid
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets with some vegetable matter, spirulina flake
items.note: A bright blue mbuna that is active and territorial. It does best in a rock-heavy tank with hard, alkaline water, one male and several females, and other mbuna so the aggression is spread out.
tips: Do not keep a single female with a male; use a harem.
Stack rocks securely so they cannot collapse.
Overstock with mbuna of similar size to spread aggression.

items.name: Lemon Cichlid
items.social: Pair or small group in a large tank
items.diet: Carnivore-leaning omnivore: small pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A bright yellow-orange Tanganyikan cave spawner. It defends its cave from tankmates, so give it rockwork with plenty of hiding places, hard alkaline water and a tight-fitting lid.
tips: Provide caves; it breeds and defends in them.
