Needs hard, alkaline water.
Choose tankmates that are not tiny or timid.

items.name: Princess of Burundi
items.diet: Omnivore: small pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: A graceful Tanganyikan cichlid with long, lace-like fins that lives in family groups and tends fry together. Provide rockwork with caves, hard alkaline water and a long tank.
tips: Provide rockwork and caves.
Needs hard, alkaline water.
Offspring may stay with the parents and help guard the nest.

items.name: Celebes Rainbowfish
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: A slender, graceful fish with yellow-edged fins and an elegant sail on males. Related to rainbowfish but from Sulawesi, it prefers harder, alkaline water and a long tank with plenty of open swimming room.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Use a tight lid; they jump.
Prefers harder, alkaline water over soft tap water.

items.name: Turquoise Rainbowfish
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A deep-bodied rainbowfish with blue-turquoise color over a darker back. It is active, peaceful and good in a long community tank with hard, alkaline water, and it needs a lid.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Use a tight lid.
Give it a long tank, not just a tall one.

items.name: Giraffe Cichlid
items.temperament: Predatory ambush hunter, aggressive to small fish
items.social: Solitary male with females in a very large tank
items.diet: Carnivore: large cichlid pellets, frozen fish and shrimp
items.note: A big Malawi predator with a giraffe-like pattern that lies still on its side to ambush small fish. Juveniles look harmless in the store, but adults reach about ten inches and eat any fish small enough to swallow.
tips: Plan for a tank of 125 gallons or larger before buying.
Do not mix with small tankmates.
Choose large, sturdy Malawi tankmates.

items.name: Kerri Danio
items.origin: Islands and coastal mainland of southwestern Thailand
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A slim, blue-sheened danio from a small corner of coastal Thailand. It is calmer and less frantic than a zebra danio, and a bigger group brings out the males' color and settles the whole school down.
tips: Keep a group of eight or more.
Use a tight lid; it jumps like other danios.
Plants and some current suit its stream habitat.

items.name: Wrestling Halfbeak
items.origin: South and Southeast Asia, including slow and brackish-tinged waters
items.temperament: Peaceful toward other species; males spar with each other
items.social: Groups; one male or several, not just two
items.diet: Carnivore: fruit flies, small live and frozen foods; may ignore dry food
items.note: A livebearer that spends nearly all its time at the surface hunting small insects, with a pointed lower jaw unlike a guppy or platy. Males joust with each other over territory, so keep either a single male or a real group rather than two that will fixate on one another, and expect it to be flighty until it settles in.
tips: Feed from the surface; it rarely looks lower in the tank.
Use a tight lid and dense edge planting; it jumps and startles easily.
Prioritize surface area over depth when choosing a tank.

items.name: Glass Knifefish
items.temperament: Peaceful toward similar-sized fish, but will eat very small tankmates
items.social: Small group of its own kind
items.diet: Carnivore: frozen bloodworms, brine shrimp, small sinking pellets
items.note: A translucent, nearly tail-less fish that swims with an undulating ribbon-like fin and senses its surroundings with a weak electric field. It is nocturnal and shy in bright light, so keep it with calm tankmates its own size or larger and give it shaded hiding spots.
tips: Keep several together rather than just one.
Provide dim lighting and plant cover or driftwood to hide in.
Avoid tankmates small enough to be eaten after dark.

items.name: Bleher's Rainbowfish
items.origin: Lake Holmes and feeder streams, Mamberamo region, Indonesia
items.social: Schooling, keep 6+, more than one male
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A deep-bodied rainbowfish with an orange back fading to blue, from a single lake system in Indonesia. Keeping more than one male in the group brings out brighter color and more natural display behavior than a single male alone.
tips: Keep at least two males with several females.
Needs a long tank with open swimming room.
Likes hard, alkaline water, which suits San Diego tap well.

items.name: Variatus Platy
items.social: Groups with more females than males
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods, blanched vegetables or algae
items.note: A hardy, colorful livebearer that tolerates cooler water than many tropical fish. Males chase females constantly, so keep two or three females per male, and expect fry in a planted tank.
tips: Keep more females than males.
Prefers harder, neutral to alkaline water, which suits San Diego tap water.
Give it plants and cover so fry and females can rest.

items.name: African Butterfly Cichlid
items.diet: Omnivore: small pellets, flakes, frozen and live foods
items.note: A small, peaceful West African cichlid that forms strong pairs and cares for its young. It leaves plants alone and does well in a quiet planted tank, but pairs defend a cave when breeding.
tips: Provide caves or flowerpots for spawning.
Keep calm tankmates; boisterous fish stress it.
If a pair fights, separate the weaker fish.

items.name: Rainbow Krib
items.diet: Omnivore: small pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: A dwarf cichlid related to the kribensis, with a more colorful body that varies by collection locality. Keep a pair with a cave, soft to moderately hard water and calm tankmates.
tips: Provide a cave for each pair.
Keep gentle tankmates.
Locality names (Nigeria Red, Moliwe etc.) are collection points of the same species group.

items.name: Spotted Danio
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: A small, calm danio with a blue stripe and dark spots, quieter than the zebra danio. It does best in a group on its own or with similarly small, peaceful fish, and it jumps, so use a lid.
tips: Keep a group of eight or more.
Use a tight lid.
Best with small, calm tankmates, not boisterous fish.

items.name: Ornate Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: A small tetra with a tall, white-edged dorsal fin on males. It is peaceful and does best in a group of eight or more in a planted tank with gentle flow, with live or frozen food for color and condition.
tips: Keep eight or more.
Gentle flow and plants suit it.
Avoid boisterous tankmates.

items.name: Black Shark
items.origin: Southeast Asia (Mekong and Chao Phraya basins)
items.diet: Omnivore: algae and vegetables (peas, cucumber), sinking pellets, frozen foods
items.note: Sold as a sleek black juvenile, this fish becomes a large, territorial adult about two feet long that is best suited to public aquariums or the very largest home tanks. Do not buy it for a standard community tank.
tips: Plan for a tank at least 6 ft long before buying.
Keep only one; it is aggressive to similar-shaped fish.
Not a red-tail shark or rainbow shark; those stay far smaller.

items.name: Powder Blue Socolofi Cichlid
items.temperament: Territorial but milder than many mbuna
items.diet: Mostly herbivore: spirulina flakes, vegetable pellets, some frozen foods
items.note: A soft blue mbuna that is calmer than many Malawi cichlids but still territorial. Keep one male with several females in hard, alkaline water with rockwork, and avoid pairing it with very aggressive mbuna.
tips: One male per tank unless it is large.
Needs hard, alkaline water and rock caves.
Feed plant-based foods; avoid red meats.

items.name: Sunshine Pleco (L014)
items.temperament: Relatively peaceful but can be territorial toward other bottom-dwellers; mostly nocturnal
items.social: Solitary, or one per very large tank
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets, bloodworms, shrimp, blanched vegetables; needs real protein, not just algae
items.note: A striking L-number pleco with a gold-speckled dark body, endemic to the Rio Xingu. It is sold small but grows into a large, long-lived fish that needs real swimming room and a varied, protein-rich diet, not just algae wafers.
tips: Plan for a tank of at least 80 gallons as an adult; some keepers recommend up to 125 gallons for a fully grown fish.
Feed real protein (bloodworms, shrimp) alongside vegetables; algae alone is not enough.
Keep only one per tank unless the tank is very large; it can be territorial with other bottom-dwellers.

items.name: Kitty Tetra
items.origin: Headwater streams of the Xingu and Araguaia basins, Mato Grosso, Brazil
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, daphnia, cyclops, frozen foods
items.note: A tiny, soft-water tetra from Brazil, sold in the trade as a tentative identification ('cf. loweae') rather than a fully settled species name. It is lively but shy, and hides near larger fish unless kept in a real group of its own.
tips: Keep eight or more; a lone or small group hides and stresses easily.
Soft, slightly acidic water suits it best, though it adapts to moderate hardness.
Avoid large or boisterous tankmates; it is easily outcompeted at feeding time.

items.name: Spotback Loach
items.origin: Sri Lanka (Kanneliya Forest and Gin Ganga river system)
items.temperament: Can be territorial; keep with robust, fast-swimming tankmates
items.social: Singly or a small group with room to spread out
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets, bloodworms, brine shrimp, daphnia; avoid overfeeding, it is greedy
items.note: A small Sri Lankan stream loach, also sold as the banded mountain loach, built for fast, highly oxygenated water over a pebble bottom. It is more territorial than most small loaches, so give it space and strong flow rather than a crowded, still tank.
tips: Provide strong water flow and high oxygenation, like its fast hill-stream habitat.
Use fine sand plus smooth rounded pebbles so it can dig and perch.
Give it room; it can be territorial toward its own kind in a small tank.

items.name: Scarlet Badis
items.origin: Brahmaputra River tributaries, Assam and West Bengal, India
items.temperament: Peaceful and shy, but males are territorial toward each other
items.social: Loose small groups; one male per tank unless it is large
items.diet: Carnivore (micropredator): live or frozen daphnia, cyclops, baby brine shrimp, grindal worms; most refuse flakes and pellets
items.note: One of the smallest widely kept aquarium fish, with a male rarely passing three-quarters of an inch under its vivid red-and-blue banding. It was long classified as a form of the plainer, larger Badis badis before being split into its own genus, and it still turns up under both names in the trade. It hunts tiny live prey rather than grazing on flake, so a heavily planted tank with a standing culture of small live or frozen foods suits it far better than a flake-fed community tank.
tips: Stock live or frozen daphnia, cyclops or baby brine shrimp before buying; most never learn to eat flake or pellets.
Give each male his own territory with plants or wood; two males in a small tank will fight.
Go light on bloodworms and tubifex; keepers link a steady diet of them to obesity in a fish this small.
Avoid fast or boisterous tankmates and small shrimp fry; a shy micropredator loses out at feeding time and may eat shrimp young.

items.name: African Butterflyfish
items.temperament: Peaceful with large tankmates, but eats anything small enough to swallow
items.social: Solitary or a small group in a large tank
items.diet: Carnivore: insects, crickets, small frozen foods, floating sticks or pellets once trained
items.note: A flat-backed surface fish with huge, wing-like pectoral fins. It hunts at the top of the tank, can leap out of the water, and needs a tight lid, floating plants for cover and a calm surface, not strong flow.
tips: Use a very secure lid; it can jump and glide out of the tank.
Do not keep with small fish such as neons; it will eat them.
Keep the surface calm and dim with floating plants.

items.name: Skunk Loach
items.origin: Mekong and Chao Phraya basins, Southeast Asia
items.temperament: Active, semi-aggressive toward slow or long-finned fish; sociable with its own kind
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets, frozen bloodworms and brine shrimp, snails; some blanched vegetables
items.note: A bold, striped botia loach with an orange tinge on the fins. It lives for many years, likes company and hiding places, and eats small snails. Keep it in a group on soft sand with caves, and avoid slow or long-finned tankmates.
tips: Keep a group of five or more to reduce bullying among them.
Use sand or smooth gravel and plenty of caves or wood.
It eats small snails and may chase slow fish.

items.name: Mexican Tetra
items.origin: Texas, New Mexico and Mexico (surface form); caves in Mexico (blind form)
items.temperament: Active, may nip slow or long-finned fish
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, small pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A hardy, silvery tetra that tolerates cooler temperatures than most tropical tetras. The sighted form and the pale, eyeless blind cave form are the same species. Blind fish do well with calm tankmates and an unchanged tank layout.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Avoid long-finned or slow tankmates; they may be nipped.
Blind fish find food by smell and touch; do not rearrange the tank often.

items.name: Blue Dolphin Cichlid
items.temperament: Peaceful for its size, but eats small fish and is easily outcompeted by aggressive mbuna
items.social: One male with females, or a single fish
items.diet: Carnivore/omnivore: quality cichlid pellets, frozen mysis and brine shrimp, krill
items.note: A large, peaceful Lake Malawi cichlid known for the rounded hump on the male's forehead. It is a sand-sifting hunter in the wild and does best in hard, alkaline water with open swimming space and calm tankmates, not boisterous mbuna.
tips: Plan for a tank of 100 gallons or more as an adult.
Do not mix with very aggressive mbuna; it is slow to feed and gets bullied.
Do not keep with small fish it can swallow.

items.name: Banded Archerfish
items.origin: Estuaries and mangroves from India to Australia
items.temperament: Peaceful with similar-sized fish; eats small fish and insects
items.social: Groups in a large tank, or single
items.diet: Carnivore: insects, crickets, shrimp, small frozen foods, sinking or floating pellets
items.note: A surface-hunting fish famous for spitting jets of water at insects. Juveniles are sold in fresh water, but adults need brackish water to stay healthy, and they need a long tank with open space at the surface and a lid with a small gap.
tips: Plan on brackish water (slightly salty) as they grow; do not keep long term in pure fresh water.
Use a long tank and keep the water level a few inches below the lid.
Do not keep with small fish; it can swallow tankmates.

items.name: Bumblebee Goby
items.origin: Southeast Asian estuaries and mangrove streams
items.temperament: Peaceful but territorial with its own kind
items.diet: Carnivore: live or frozen foods such as baby brine shrimp, daphnia and bloodworms; usually refuses dry food
items.note: A tiny yellow-and-black goby that perches on wood and rocks. It is often sold as a freshwater fish but does best in lightly brackish water, and many will only accept live or frozen foods, so it is not a beginner fish.
tips: Provide brackish water (a pinch of aquarium salt is not enough; use marine salt mix to the right gravity).
Confirm it eats frozen foods before bringing it home.
Give each goby a cave or a flowerpot to claim.

items.name: Orange Chromide
items.origin: India and Sri Lanka (fresh and brackish water)
items.temperament: Peaceful, a little territorial when breeding
items.diet: Omnivore: small pellets, frozen foods, brine shrimp, some vegetable matter
items.note: A small, colorful cichlid that lives in fresh and brackish water. It does best in hard, alkaline water with a little marine salt added and quiet tankmates. It is peaceful, and pairs raise eggs on a flat surface.
tips: Hard, slightly brackish water keeps it healthiest.
Keep a pair or a group with plenty of hiding spots.
Avoid fast, boisterous tankmates.

items.name: Dawn Tetra
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: A tiny, peaceful tetra with a golden-orange glow and a faint stripe through the tail. It is a good match for small planted community tanks and other gentle fish.
tips: Keep a group of eight or more.
Choose small, calm tankmates.
Stable, clean water keeps the color bright.

items.name: Brilliant Rasbora
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, small frozen foods
items.note: A slim, peaceful schooling rasbora with a bright red-orange tail and a dark stripe along the side. It is hardy and easy, shows best color in a group of eight or more, and likes a planted tank with open water for swimming.
tips: Keep a group of eight or more.
Use a snug lid; rasboras can jump.
Pair with other small, calm fish.

items.name: Forktail Blue-Eye
items.diet: Micro pellets, baby brine shrimp, small frozen and live foods
items.note: A tiny, bright yellow-and-blue rainbowfish relative with a forked tail and pale blue eyes. It does best in a group in a planted tank with neutral to slightly alkaline, clean water, and it suits calm nano community setups.
tips: Keep a group of six or more, with more females than males.
Avoid soft, acidic water.
Feed small portions; it is a tiny mouth.

items.name: Cyprichromis (Blue Flash and Jumbo Cyps)
items.diet: Omnivore: small cichlid pellets, flakes, frozen foods, mysis
items.note: A slim, active Tanganyikan cichlid that swims in schools in open water instead of hiding in caves. It needs a long tank, hard alkaline water and a good-sized group, and it should only be kept with other calm fish.
tips: Keep ten or more so the school looks natural.
Use a long tank with open swimming space and rock at the sides.
Keep with peaceful tankmates; rowdy cichlids stress it.

items.name: Peacock Gudgeon
items.diet: Omnivore: small pellets, frozen foods, live foods, crushed flakes
items.note: A small, colorful bottom-to-mid fish with a spotted tail and a pink-and-blue sheen. It is a calm, easy choice for a planted community tank with caves, and it will use a small cave to spawn.
tips: Provide small caves or pipes.
Choose calm tankmates; larger fish steal the food.
Offer sinking and frozen foods as well as flakes.

items.name: Sheepshead Acara
items.temperament: Peaceful for a cichlid, pairs defend a territory when breeding
items.social: Pair or small group in a large tank
items.diet: Omnivore: small cichlid pellets, frozen foods, flakes
items.note: A small, calm South American dwarf cichlid with a tan to bluish body and a dark side spot. It is a good fit for a planted community tank with gentle, similar-sized fish, and a bonded pair will clean a flat stone or leaf and guard the eggs.
tips: Keep a pair rather than several males.
Very small fish and fry may be eaten, so choose tankmates of similar size.
Provide a flat rock or cave for spawning and keep the water clean.

items.name: Golden Dwarf Cichlid
items.origin: Guyana and Suriname, northern South America
items.temperament: Peaceful out of breeding, males can be territorial
items.social: Pair or one male with several females
items.diet: Omnivore: small pellets, frozen foods, live foods, flakes
items.note: A small dwarf cichlid with a golden-green body. Females turn bright yellow with dark bands when ready to breed, and they guard the eggs in a cave. Keep one male per tank unless it is large and well decorated.
tips: One male per tank; males fight.
Provide small caves and dense plants.
Needs a tight lid; males can jump when chasing.

items.name: Black Belt Cichlid
items.social: Solitary or a mated pair in a very large tank
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, vegetable foods, frozen foods
items.note: A big, strong Central American cichlid sold small but growing to a foot or more. It is a digger with a bad temper toward other cichlids, so it needs a large tank, heavy equipment and tankmates that can handle it.
tips: Plan for a tank of 125 gallons or more for an adult.
Secure rocks and equipment; it digs and moves decor.
Do not mix with small or timid fish.

items.name: Calvus Cichlid
items.temperament: Semi-aggressive toward its own kind, hunts tiny fish
items.social: Pair or small harem in a larger tank
items.diet: Carnivore: small frozen foods such as mysis and brine shrimp, small pellets
items.note: A slender Tanganyikan cichlid with a tall back and bold white or black patterning. It lives among rock crevices, hunts small prey and breeds in caves. It needs hard, alkaline water and rock work with many hiding places.
tips: Build rock caves and crevices; it hides and ambushes from them.
Keep water hard and alkaline.
Do not mix with fry or very small fish.

items.name: Cuckoo Catfish
items.temperament: Peaceful to semi-aggressive, may eat small fish
items.social: Groups of 3+ in a larger tank, or solitary
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets, frozen foods, vegetable matter
items.note: A spotted, big-headed Tanganyikan catfish best known for laying its eggs among those of mouthbrooding cichlids. In a tank it does well with hard, alkaline water and cichlid tankmates, and needs caves to rest in during the day.
tips: Pair with Tanganyikan or Malawi cichlids, which like the same hard water.
Provide caves; it is more active at night.
Do not keep with tiny fish; the mouth is large.

items.name: Florida Flagfish
items.temperament: Peaceful to semi-aggressive; males are territorial
items.social: Pair or one male with several females
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, plenty of algae and vegetable matter
items.note: A hardy native killifish relative from Florida with a red-spotted, greenish body and a dark tail spot. It eats soft algae and tolerates cool to warm water, but males can be pushy toward each other and other small fish.
tips: Keep one male with several females.
Offer vegetable foods or algae to keep it healthy.
May nip fins of long-finned tankmates.

items.name: Texas Cichlid
items.origin: Rio Grande basin, Texas and northeastern Mexico
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, frozen foods, some vegetable matter
items.note: A stocky, pearl-spotted cichlid from the Rio Grande area. It is a bold, digging, territorial fish that outgrows most home tanks, so give it a large tank, strong filtration and tankmates that can hold their own.
tips: A pair needs 75 gallons at minimum; more if there are tankmates.
Expect digging; secure rocks and keep plants in pots.
Keep it with similarly sized, sturdy fish, not small community fish.

items.name: Rainbow Cichlid
items.origin: Honduras to Costa Rica, Central America
items.social: Pair or small group in a large tank
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, frozen foods, vegetable matter
items.note: A small Central American cichlid that changes from a plain, barred look to a bright yellow-orange when breeding. It is hardy and active, eats plants if it can, and gets pushy at spawning time.
tips: Use a 55 gallon or larger tank with rocks and caves.
Choose tankmates of similar size and toughness.
Expect it to nibble soft plants.

items.name: Livingston's Cichlid
items.social: Solitary or one male with several females
items.diet: Carnivore: cichlid pellets, frozen fish and shrimp, occasional live food
items.note: A mottled Lake Malawi predator known for lying on its side as if dead, then striking any small fish that comes to investigate. It needs a large tank with hard, alkaline water and only large, robust tankmates.
tips: Plan for a 125 gallon or larger tank.
Do not keep with small fish or fry; it will eat them.
Use Malawi-type hard, alkaline water and plenty of rock cover.

items.name: Saulosi Cichlid
items.diet: Omnivore: mbuna pellets and flakes with vegetable matter
items.note: A small rock-dwelling Malawi cichlid. Males are blue with dark bars and females are bright yellow, so a group of mostly females with one male looks great and spreads out male aggression.
tips: Keep one male with several females.
Use rockwork with plenty of caves and hard, alkaline water.
Offer mostly vegetable-based food and avoid too much protein.

items.name: Redtail Splitfin
items.temperament: Peaceful but males can be pushy
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, small pellets, frozen foods, algae and vegetable matter
items.note: A hardy goodeid livebearer with a blue-black body and an orange-red tail on the males. It prefers hard, alkaline water and cooler tropical temperatures, and the young are born well developed.
tips: Keep more females than males to spread out chasing.
Use hard water and avoid very warm temperatures.
Offer vegetable matter or algae; it grazes.

items.name: Butterfly Goodeid
items.temperament: Peaceful but fins may be nipped; males chase
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, small pellets, frozen foods, algae and vegetable matter
items.note: A silvery, black-spotted livebearer whose males have a yellow-edged tail. It is a gentle fish that likes hard, alkaline water, and it may nibble the fins of slow, long-finned tankmates.
tips: Use hard water and keep the tank cooler than a typical tropical setup.
Keep a group with more females than males.
Add vegetable foods or algae to the diet.

items.name: Pagoda Snail
items.diet: Algae, biofilm, sinking pellets, blanched vegetables
items.note: A small snail with a tall, ridged spiral shell, kept for its looks and for eating algae and leftovers. It gives birth to a few live young rather than laying egg clusters, so numbers rise slowly. It prefers clean, well-oxygenated, slightly cooler water.
tips: Avoid copper medications; snails are sensitive to them.
Keep the water clean and well oxygenated.
Provide calcium sources so the shell stays healthy.

items.name: Banded Leporinus
items.origin: Amazon and Orinoco basins, South America
items.temperament: Semi-aggressive; chases its own kind, eats soft plants
items.social: Small group in a big tank, or solitary
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets, vegetables, blanched greens, frozen foods
items.note: A bold, striped fish that is sold small but grows to about a foot long. It is fast, jumps, and shreds soft plants, so it fits a large tank with sturdy tankmates rather than a typical community setup.
tips: Plan for a large, long tank with a tight lid.
Expect it to eat soft plants; offer vegetables daily.
Do not mix with small fish or timid fish.

items.name: Fire Eel
items.temperament: Peaceful with large fish, eats anything it can swallow
items.diet: Carnivore: earthworms, frozen foods, shrimp, fish pieces
items.note: A long, dramatic spiny eel sold small that grows to well over two feet. It buries in sand, escapes through the smallest gap, and needs a very large, long tank, so it is a fish to plan for rather than an impulse buy.
tips: Use fine sand and cover every gap in the lid.
Do not keep with small fish or shrimp; it may eat them.
Use medications and salt carefully; eels are sensitive.

items.name: Pink-Tail Chalceus
items.social: Small group in a very large tank, or solitary
items.diet: Carnivore: pellets, frozen fish and shrimp, insects
items.note: A fast, silver, torpedo-shaped fish with a pink-orange tail that grows about a foot long. It is a strong jumper and will eat small tankmates, so it needs a long tank, a heavy lid and large, quick tankmates.
tips: Use a heavy, tight-fitting lid.
Avoid small fish; they become food.
Give it a long tank for swimming room.

items.name: Royal Farlowella
items.diet: Herbivore: algae wafers, blanched vegetables, biofilm on wood
items.note: A slim, twig-like armored catfish with long tail filaments. It is gentle and eats algae and soft vegetables, but it needs clean, well-oxygenated water and should be introduced to a mature tank.
tips: Offer wood and blanched vegetables.
Keep the water clean and well oxygenated.
Avoid rowdy tankmates that outcompete it for food.

items.name: Rosy Bitterling
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, small frozen foods
items.note: A small, peaceful coldwater-to-cool schooling fish with a pink flush on breeding males. It does well without a heater in a planted tank, but it breeds only with a freshwater mussel, which is a specialist keeping project.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Does not need a heater in most homes; avoid very warm water.
Breeding requires a live freshwater mussel; do not add one casually.

items.name: Clown Barb
items.origin: Borneo and nearby islands, Southeast Asia
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, flakes, vegetables, frozen foods
items.note: A larger, vivid barb with orange fins and bold dark blotches. It is active and boisterous, eats soft plants, and does best in a group with similar-sized, sturdy tankmates.
tips: Keep six or more to spread out aggression.
Avoid long-finned or timid tankmates.
Offer vegetables; it nibbles soft plants.

items.name: Compressiceps Cichlid
items.temperament: Predatory toward small fish and fry; territorial
items.social: Pair or small group in a large tank
items.diet: Carnivore: frozen foods, small live foods, sinking cichlid pellets
items.note: A laterally flattened Tanganyikan cichlid that slips between rocks and hunts small prey. It needs hard, alkaline water, lots of rock caves and a calm, rock-oriented tank.
tips: Use hard, alkaline water and plenty of rock caves.
Keep away from small fish and fry.
Feed small, varied meals.

items.name: Brevis Shell Dweller
items.diet: Carnivore: small frozen foods, baby brine shrimp, micro pellets
items.note: A tiny Tanganyikan shell-dweller that lives and breeds in empty snail shells. It uses hard, alkaline water and a sandy bottom with plenty of shells.
tips: Use fine sand and scatter empty snail shells.
Use hard, alkaline water.
Feed small foods; it is tiny.

items.name: Bumblebee Cichlid
items.social: Groups in a large tank, or pair
items.diet: Omnivore leaning carnivore: cichlid pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A striped, bumblebee-patterned Malawi cichlid that grows larger than most mbuna. It needs rocks, hard, alkaline water and a roomy tank to spread out territorial behavior.
tips: Use rock caves and hard, alkaline water.
Provide a larger tank than a typical mbuna.
Choose robust tankmates.

items.name: Maingano Cichlid
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, spirulina flakes, vegetables
items.note: A small, active mbuna from Lake Malawi, with males blue and barred and females golden. Like most mbuna it is territorial and does best in a rocky tank with other Malawi fish.
tips: Use rock caves and hard, alkaline water.
Overstock lightly with similar fish to spread aggression.
Do not mix with calm community fish.

items.name: Mono (Moony)
items.origin: Coastal waters, estuaries and river mouths of the Indo-Pacific and West Africa
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods, blanched vegetables
items.note: A tall, silver, disc-shaped fish that is often sold as a juvenile in plain freshwater. Adults do much better in brackish water, and many keepers move them toward full marine strength over time. They are active schooling fish that need a large tank with open swimming space.
tips: Plan to raise the salinity gradually; do not keep adults long term in plain freshwater.
Use a salt mix made for aquariums and measure with a hydrometer or refractometer.
Keep a group of three or more in a long tank; avoid small tankmates that fit in the mouth.

items.name: Scat (Ruby and Green)
items.origin: Coastal mangroves, estuaries and river mouths, Indo-Pacific
items.temperament: Peaceful but bold; eats plants and small fish
items.social: Groups of 3+ in a large tank
items.diet: Omnivore: vegetables, algae wafers, pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A round, spotted fish sold young in freshwater, with the ruby form showing red patches. Adults grow larger than many buyers expect and do best in brackish water. They nibble plants, so real plants rarely last.
tips: Move toward brackish water as the fish grows; juveniles tolerate freshwater, adults decline in it.
Handle with care; the fin spines can sting.
Plan for a long, spacious tank for the adult size.

items.name: Graceful Mudskipper
items.social: One, or a small group in a large paludarium
items.diet: Carnivore: live and frozen insects, bloodworms, small shrimp
items.note: A fish that leaves the water and hops across mud. It needs a paludarium: shallow brackish water, a large mud or sand land area, warm humid air and a very tight lid. It is not a fish for an ordinary tank.
tips: At least half the setup must be damp land they can climb onto.
Use brackish water and keep the air warm and humid.
Offer live or frozen foods on land; they will not eat dry flake in the water.

items.name: Pike Characin
items.origin: Amazon and Orinoco basins, South America
items.social: Solitary or a pair in a very large tank
items.diet: Carnivore: live or frozen fish, shrimp, large insects
items.note: A slim, fast surface hunter that looks like a small gar. It can leap, bolts when startled and damages itself easily, so it needs a long, covered tank and calm handling. Many wild-type fish start on live foods and need patience to switch.
tips: Use a long tank with a heavy, tight lid.
Do not house with fish small enough to swallow.
Keep lighting dim and avoid sudden movement near the glass.

items.name: Wood Catfish
items.diet: Carnivore: sinking pellets, frozen bloodworms, brine shrimp
items.note: A small, spotted, nocturnal catfish that hides in wood and caves by day. It is easy once settled in a dim tank with plenty of cover, and it should not be kept with very tiny fish it could swallow.
tips: Provide wood, caves and dim areas to hide in.
Feed after lights out or sink food near hiding places.
Keep a group so they feel secure.
aka: milky way wood catfish tatia galaxias

items.name: Garra Gotyla
items.origin: Rivers and streams of India and the Himalayan foothills
items.diet: Herbivore: algae wafers, spirulina, blanched vegetables, biofilm
items.note: A rock-clinging algae grazer that uses a sucker-like mouth. It likes cooler, well-oxygenated, moderate-flow water and does best in a mature tank with algae-covered rock.
tips: Provide strong flow and plenty of oxygen.
Offer vegetable foods and algae-covered rocks.
Keep a group; singles can be shy.

items.name: Cactus and Leopard Plecos (L155, L114)
items.origin: Amazon and Orinoco basins, South America
items.temperament: Territorial, spiny; peaceful with fish too big to bother
items.diet: Carnivore and omnivore: meaty sinking foods, shrimp, wood, some vegetables
items.note: Large, spiny, predatory-leaning plecos with striking spots or colored fin edges. They are sold as small juveniles but need a very large tank, strong filtration and hard hiding places when adult. They are also quite spiny, so use caution when netting.
tips: Plan for a 150-gallon or larger tank before buying a juvenile.
Keep only one per tank unless the tank is huge.
Feed meaty sinking foods; provide caves and wood.
aka: l155 polka dot lyretail pleco acanthicus adonis

items.name: Stiphodon Goby
items.social: Small group with a hide for each male
items.diet: Grazer: biofilm and algae on rocks, plus frozen foods
items.note: A tiny, brightly colored grazing goby from fast streams. It needs a mature, algae-covered tank with strong flow, high oxygen and a tight lid. Many are wild-caught and delicate, so this is a specialist fish.
tips: Only add to a mature tank with growing algae and biofilm.
Provide strong flow, oxygen and a tight lid.
Offer small frozen foods in addition to grazing.

items.name: Bladder Snail
items.diet: Algae, detritus, leftover food, biofilm
items.note: A tiny, fast-breeding snail that arrives on plants and cleans up scraps and film. It is harmless to plants and fish but will multiply quickly if the tank is overfed.
tips: Feed less to slow population growth.
Needs calcium in the water for a healthy shell.
Avoid copper medications.

items.name: Rosy Red Minnow
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, small pellets, frozen foods
items.note: The rosy red minnow is a pink color form of the fathead minnow. It is a hardy, cool-water fish that does well unheated and works in cool-water tanks and ponds, but it is not a fit for a warm tropical community.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Prefers cool water; avoid tropical heat.
Often sold as a feeder, but is a fine pet fish.

items.name: Sailfin Tetra
items.origin: Guianas and Amazon basin, South America
items.diet: Carnivore: small frozen and live foods, micro pellets
items.note: A tetra relative with a long sail-like dorsal fin and a dark tail spot. It prefers soft, acidic, tannin-tinted water with plenty of cover and gentle tankmates.
tips: Use plants, wood and subdued light.
Keep water soft and clean.
Males may display at each other; give hiding spots.

items.name: Splash Tetra
items.diet: Carnivore: micro pellets, flakes, small frozen and live foods
items.note: A surface-oriented fish famous for laying eggs on leaves above the water. It jumps, so it needs a snug lid with a little humid air gap, and it does best in soft, slightly acidic water.
tips: Keep a snug lid; it jumps.
Choose gentle tankmates.
Feed small foods at the surface.

items.name: Lionhead Cichlid
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking cichlid pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A stocky, bottom-hugging Congo cichlid with a bump on the forehead. It lacks a normal swim bladder, so it hops across the bottom, and it likes rocks, caves and fast water flow.
tips: Provide caves and rockwork.
Use moderate to strong current.
Keep with similar-sized, sturdy fish; it guards its cave.

items.name: Goby Cichlid
items.social: Pairs or groups in a larger tank
items.diet: Omnivore: algae-based foods, small frozen foods, small pellets
items.note: A small Tanganyikan cichlid that perches on rocks and grazes algae, shaped much like a goby. It needs hard, alkaline water, rocky structure and good flow.
tips: Use rockwork with plenty of surfaces to graze.
Keep water hard, alkaline and well oxygenated.
Do not mix with soft-water fish.

items.name: Afra Cichlid
items.diet: Omnivore: algae-based cichlid pellets, flakes, occasional frozen foods
items.note: A blue-barred mbuna from Lake Malawi, usually sold under collection-site names. Like other mbuna it is territorial and does best in a rocky tank with hard, alkaline water.
tips: Overstock lightly with other mbuna to spread aggression.
Use rock caves and hard, alkaline water.
Avoid mixing with peaceful community fish.

items.name: Kadango Red Fin Cichlid
items.social: Group with one male and several females
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: A Malawi hap with a blue body and bright red fins on males. It is calmer than mbuna but males squabble, so keep one male with several females in a roomy tank.
tips: Keep one male with several females.
Use hard, alkaline water.
Give open swimming space as well as rocks.

items.name: Emerald Cichlid
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, frozen foods, vegetables
items.note: A large, deep-bodied South American cichlid that is usually calmer than other big cichlids but will eat small fish. It needs a big tank, strong filtration and regular water changes.
tips: Plan for a tank of 125 gallons or more.
Do not keep with small fish.
Keep up with water changes; waste builds fast.

items.name: Jaguar Cichlid (Managua Cichlid)
items.origin: Honduras to Costa Rica, Central America
items.social: Solitary or a mated pair in a very large tank
items.diet: Carnivore: large cichlid pellets, fish, shrimp, earthworms
items.note: A powerful, spotted Central American predator that grows over a foot long. It is bold and intelligent but bullies and eats tankmates, so it needs a very large tank and heavy equipment.
tips: Plan for 180 gallons or more.
Keep only with similarly large, tough fish, or alone.
Use a secure lid and strong filtration; do regular big water changes.

items.name: African Lungfish
items.diet: Carnivore: shrimp, earthworms, chunks of fish, sinking carnivore pellets
items.note: An eel-like air-breathing fish that grows far longer than juveniles in the store suggest. It can escape through small gaps and eats any fish it can swallow, so it needs a long tank with a heavy lid and an air gap above the water.
tips: Secure the lid; it climbs and escapes.
Leave an air gap so it can breathe at the surface.
Keep alone or with fish too large to eat.

items.name: African Tigerfish
items.social: Solitary or in a very large tank
items.diet: Carnivore: whole live or frozen fish, large prey foods
items.note: A fast open-water predator with very sharp teeth. It is easily stressed, needs a huge long tank with strong flow and excellent water quality, and is not a fish for a typical home setup.
tips: Only for experienced keepers with a very large tank.
Handle nets and tank work carefully; the teeth cut.
Keep the tank long, open and spotless; it spooks and injures itself easily.

items.name: Indian Glassfish
items.diet: Carnivore: small frozen and live foods, micro pellets once trained
items.note: A see-through schooling fish with a faint blue sheen on males. It does best in a group in hard, neutral-to-alkaline water, and many fish take a while to accept dry food. Brightly colored 'painted' glassfish have been artificially dyed; their color fades, so choose natural fish.
tips: Keep six or more together.
Offer frozen or live foods first, then train to small pellets.
Prefers harder water; very soft, acidic water is a poor fit.

items.name: Red Empress Cichlid
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, flakes, frozen foods
items.note: A Lake Malawi haplochromine whose male turns orange-red over a blue-grey body. It is calmer than mbuna but males squabble, so keep a single male with several females in a roomy tank with hard, alkaline water.
tips: Keep one male with several females.
Provide rocks plus open swimming space.
Use hard, alkaline water and regular water changes.

items.name: Ocellatus Shell Dweller
items.temperament: Territorial toward its own kind, small and bold
items.social: Pair or colony in a 20 gal or larger
items.diet: Carnivore: small frozen foods, baby brine shrimp, fine pellets
items.note: A tiny Tanganyikan cichlid that lives in empty snail shells on a sand bottom. It is feisty for its size, needs hard, alkaline water, and spends its day defending its shell and the sand around it.
tips: Provide one or more empty snail shells per fish and a deep sand bed.
Keep water hard and alkaline.
Choose tankmates that stay out of the bottom territory.

items.name: Egyptian Mouthbrooder
items.social: Pair or one male with several females
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, small pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A small, hardy African cichlid in which the female holds eggs and fry in her mouth. It adapts to a wide range of water and suits a calm tank with plants and rocks.
tips: Keep one male with several females.
Provide caves and plants for retreat.
Avoid pairing with fish small enough to eat fry.

items.name: Rusty Cichlid
items.social: Group, one male with several females
items.diet: Omnivore: spirulina-based cichlid pellets and flakes, occasional frozen foods
items.note: A rust-orange and lavender mbuna that is one of the calmer Lake Malawi rock-dwellers. It is still territorial, so give it rockwork and hard, alkaline water.
tips: Use plenty of rocks and caves.
Keep one male with several females.
Feed mostly vegetable-based foods.

items.name: Scrapermouth Mbuna
items.social: Group in a heavily rocked tank
items.diet: Herbivore-leaning: spirulina flakes and pellets, vegetables; avoid heavy protein
items.note: A sturdy Malawi rock-dweller with a fleshy snout built for scraping algae off stone. It is territorial and does best with other mbuna in a tank with lots of rockwork, hard water and a plant-based diet.
tips: Feed vegetable-based foods; too much protein causes bloat.
Use stacked rockwork with many caves.
Do not mix with calm, soft-water fish.

items.name: Ticto Barb
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods, some vegetable matter
items.note: A silver barb with two dark spots, the male showing red on the fins in good condition. Hardy and active, it prefers a group and a longer tank rather than a tall one.
tips: Keep six or more together.
Avoid long-finned, slow tankmates.
Use a lid; barbs jump.

items.name: Banded Gourami
items.social: Single male with females or one per tank
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods, some vegetables
items.note: A hardy gourami with blue and orange diagonal bands on males. It is larger and more territorial than a dwarf gourami, and a lid with an air gap lets it breathe from the surface.
tips: Keep only one male per tank unless it is large and planted.
Leave an air gap under the lid.
Floating plants help shy fish feel secure.

items.name: Red Line Rasbora
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, flakes, small frozen foods
items.note: A slim, graceful rasbora with a red-orange stripe running the length of the body. It is a calm schooling fish for planted community tanks, best in a group of eight or more with floating plants for cover and a lid, since it can jump.
tips: Keep eight or more together.
Choose calm, small tankmates.
Use a lid; rasboras jump.

items.name: African Brown Knifefish
items.origin: Tropical Africa, from West Africa to the Nile and Congo basins
items.temperament: Peaceful with similar-sized fish, eats small tankmates; shy
items.social: Solitary or small group in a large tank
items.level: Mid to lower, hides by day
items.diet: Carnivore: frozen bloodworms, krill, chopped shrimp, sinking pellets
items.note: A slim, night-active knifefish that glides backward and forward using its long fin and breathes air at the surface. It is far smaller than the clown knife, but it hides by day, hunts by smell at night, and will eat tiny fish such as neons.
tips: Provide caves, wood or pipes to hide in.
Leave an air gap under the lid; it gulps air.
Do not keep with fish small enough to swallow.

items.name: Chinese High-Fin Banded Shark
items.social: Solitary or small group in a very large tank or pond
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets, algae wafers, blanched vegetables, frozen foods
items.note: A sail-finned juvenile that looks like a small, striped shark but is a cool-water sucker, not a tropical fish or a true shark. It grows from a few inches to two feet or more, loses much of its tall sail as it ages, and does best in cooler, well-oxygenated water, so plan a pond or a very large tank before buying.
tips: Keep it cooler than a tropical tank; low-70s or below is better.
Plan for a pond or a tank of several hundred gallons for an adult.
Provide strong filtration and plenty of oxygen.

items.name: Cape Lopez Lyretail Killifish
items.origin: Gabon and nearby coastal West Africa
items.social: Trio or small group, one male with females
items.diet: Carnivore: baby brine shrimp, daphnia, small frozen foods, fine pellets
items.note: A small, colorful killifish with a lyre-shaped tail and a gold, red-spotted body. It does best in a quiet, softer-water planted tank with a lid, and it prefers live or frozen foods to dry food.
tips: Use a tight lid; killifish jump.
Keep one male with two or three females.
Keep the water cooler and soft, with plants and floating cover.

items.name: Blue Gularis Killifish
items.origin: Niger Delta and southwestern Cameroon, West Africa
items.temperament: Active, will eat small fish; males fight
items.social: Pair or trio in a 20 gal or larger
items.diet: Carnivore: live and frozen foods, brine shrimp, bloodworms, large flakes
items.note: One of the largest and most colorful killifish, the male has a blue body with red markings and fan-shaped fins. It hunts small tankmates, jumps well, and needs a long, covered, softer-water tank with floating plants.
tips: Use a tight lid; gularis are strong jumpers.
Keep only one male per tank.
Do not house with fish small enough to eat.

items.name: Nicaragua Cichlid
items.origin: Lake Nicaragua and nearby rivers, Central America
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, frozen foods, vegetables, live foods
items.note: A hardy Central American cichlid with a tan to yellow body and dark bars, the male growing a pronounced forehead. It is one of the calmer large cichlids, but it will claim a territory and eat small tankmates, so choose fish of similar size.
tips: Provide caves and open swimming space.
Do not keep with fish small enough to swallow.
Use strong filtration and regular large water changes.

items.name: Leopard Bush Fish
items.temperament: Ambush predator, eats small fish; shy
items.diet: Carnivore: live and frozen foods, krill, bloodworms, sinking pellets once trained
items.note: A spotted labyrinth fish that waits among plants and wood and eats anything that fits in its mouth. It is calm toward larger tankmates, needs a heavily planted tank, and should have an air gap under the lid.
tips: Do not keep with fish small enough to swallow.
Leave an air gap under the lid.
Use dim light and plenty of plants, wood or caves for cover.

items.name: Amazon Leaf Fish
items.diet: Carnivore: live feeder fish, shrimp, often hard to switch to frozen foods
items.note: A leaf-mimic ambush predator that drifts head-down and snaps up small fish whole. It is shy and slow, so it should be alone or with fish that are too large to eat but too gentle to bully it. Many specimens only accept live food, which is the main reason it suits experienced keepers.
tips: Plan on live food; many refuse frozen and dry.
Keep with calm tankmates too large to swallow.
Keep the tank dim, planted and softer, with a gentle current.

items.name: Adolfo's Cory
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets and wafers, frozen and live foods
items.note: A small, popular corydoras with a white body, a dark patch behind the head and a bright orange band over the top of the head. Like other corys it is happiest in a group on soft sand with sinking food, and several look-alike species are sold under similar names.
tips: Keep five or more together.
Use sand or smooth fine gravel so the barbels stay healthy.
Feed sinking foods so it is not outcompeted by upper-level fish.

items.name: Arulius Barb
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, frozen foods, some vegetable matter
items.note: A fast, elegant barb with a long, flowing dorsal fin on adult males and bold dark bars. It is much more active and bigger than a cherry or checker barb, so give it a long tank, strong flow and a group.
tips: Keep six or more to spread out chasing.
Use a long tank with open swimming space and a tight lid.
Avoid very slow or long-finned tankmates.

items.name: Peaceful Betta
items.temperament: Calmer than a Siamese fighting fish, but males still spar
items.social: One male per tank, or a pair
items.diet: Carnivore: micro pellets, frozen and live foods such as brine shrimp and daphnia
items.note: A small wild-type betta with a shimmering body, a crescent-shaped tail and a gentler nature than the common fighting betta. Males still defend a territory against other male bettas, so keep one male per tank, and use a planted tank with floating cover and a gap under the lid.
tips: Keep one male per tank unless it is large and heavily planted.
Leave an air gap under the lid.
Use gentle flow and quiet, small tankmates only.

items.name: Golden Wonder Killifish
items.temperament: Predatory toward small fish; males squabble
items.diet: Carnivore: live and frozen foods, some pellets
items.note: A golden, striped surface hunter from India and Sri Lanka that is big enough to swallow neon-sized fish. It is a jumper that stays at the top, so it needs a very secure lid and tankmates that are much too large to eat.
tips: Use a tight lid; it is a strong jumper.
Do not keep with small fish or shrimp.
Floating plants give it cover and calm males.

items.name: Striped Headstander
items.origin: Guianas, Orinoco and Amazon basins, South America
items.temperament: Active, territorial with its own kind
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, pellets, algae wafers, blanched vegetables, frozen foods
items.note: A slim red-and-white striped fish that likes to angle head-down among plants and wood. It can bicker with its own kind, so keep it either alone or in a larger group with lots of cover, give it a long tank, and expect it to nibble soft plants.
tips: Use a tight lid; headstanders jump.
Provide wood, rocks and tall plants for territories.
Offer vegetable matter regularly.

items.name: Malawi Eye-Biter
items.temperament: Ambush predator that eats fish that fit in its mouth
items.social: Solitary or a pair in a very large tank
items.diet: Carnivore: large pellets, frozen fish and shrimp, some live foods
items.note: A long, flattened Lake Malawi predator that often lies on its side to look like a dead leaf, then strikes. Despite its nickname it does not bite eyes, but it will eat any tankmate small enough to swallow, so it is a species for a large tank with big Malawi tankmates.
tips: Do not keep with small fish or fry.
Use hard, alkaline water and rock caves.
Provide a wide, long tank; males are often aggressive to each other.

items.name: Least Killifish
items.diet: Omnivore: micro pellets, crushed flakes, baby brine shrimp, small frozen foods
items.note: One of the smallest livebearers in the world, with males under an inch. Despite its name it is a livebearer, not a true killifish. It is hardy but tiny, so only keep it with very small, gentle tankmates, and add floating plants for the young.
tips: Do not keep with fin-nippers or larger fish.
Floating plants help the tiny fry survive.
Keep a group with more females than males.

items.name: Madagascar Rainbowfish
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen and live foods
items.note: A slender, active fish from Madagascar with a black stripe and red-orange fins on males. It likes a long tank, good flow, clean water and a group, and its wild habitat is under threat, so captive-bred fish are best.
tips: Keep six or more.
Use a long tank and a tight lid.
Keep water clean and well-oxygenated; do regular water changes.

items.name: Elongatus Mbuna
items.social: Groups in a crowded mbuna tank; one male per species
items.diet: Omnivore: algae-based pellets and flakes, spirulina, small frozen foods
items.note: A slim, blue-and-black barred mbuna from Lake Malawi. Like most mbuna it is a feisty rock-dweller that does best in a rock-heavy, alkaline, overstocked-looking tank where aggression is spread out among many fish.
tips: Use hard, alkaline water and stacked rockwork.
Keep one male of each look-alike species to avoid hybrids.
Feed a vegetable-based diet in small portions.

items.name: Orange-Fin Loach
items.origin: Mekong and Chao Phraya basins, Southeast Asia
items.diet: Omnivore: sinking pellets, frozen foods, snails, some vegetables
items.note: A blue-grey, orange-finned botiid loach that grows much larger than the juveniles sold. It is active, social and hungry, will eat snails, and does best in a roomy tank with caves and a group of its own kind.
tips: Keep five or more to reduce bullying.
Provide caves and wood; it is active at dusk.
It will eat snails and may chase tiny fish.

items.name: Spotted Blue-Eye
items.origin: Aru Islands and southern New Guinea
items.diet: Micro pellets, crushed flakes, baby brine shrimp, small frozen foods
items.note: A tiny, bright-eyed rainbowfish cousin with a yellow-edged, dotted fin display. It is peaceful but very small and short-lived, so keep it in a calm planted tank with similarly small, gentle tankmates and feed tiny foods.
tips: Keep six or more; males display to each other.
Use only small, gentle tankmates and a lid.
Feed tiny foods in small portions.

items.name: Tire Track Eel
items.origin: Southeast Asia (Mekong, Chao Phraya and nearby basins)
items.temperament: Predatory toward small fish; can be territorial
items.diet: Carnivore: frozen and live foods, earthworms, chopped fish and shrimp, sinking pellets
items.note: A striking spiny eel with a tire-tread pattern that is sold small but can reach well over two feet. It hides during the day, eats any fish small enough to swallow, and needs a long, escape-proof tank with sand and plenty of caves.
tips: Plan for a long tank of 150 gallons or more for an adult.
Cover every gap; spiny eels escape through tiny openings.
Use fine sand, not sharp gravel.

items.name: Spanner Barb
items.temperament: Active, may nip smaller or long-finned fish
items.diet: Omnivore: pellets, flakes, frozen foods, blanched vegetables
items.note: A larger barb with a dark spanner- or T-shaped mark behind the head. It is active, grows well beyond the size of the juveniles in the store, and does best in a roomy tank with robust tankmates and a group of its own kind.
tips: Keep five or more to spread out nipping.
Avoid small or long-finned tankmates.
Use a long tank and tough plants; it may nibble soft ones.

items.name: Cuming's Barb
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A small, peaceful barb from Sri Lanka with an orange-red wash on the males. It is calmer than tiger barbs, likes a group and a planted tank, and tolerates a slightly cooler tropical range.
tips: Keep a group of six or more.
Use a lid; barbs can jump.
Offer some vegetable matter and small frozen foods.

items.name: Jellybean Tetra
items.diet: Micro pellets, crushed flakes, baby brine shrimp, microworms
items.note: One of the smallest tetras, a tiny, nearly see-through African fish with a red-orange flash at the tail. It is delicate and shy, so keep a good-sized group in a calm, mature, planted tank with gentle flow and only tiny, peaceful tankmates.
tips: Keep eight or more in a quiet tank.
Choose only tiny, calm tankmates.
Feed very small foods and keep water stable.

items.name: Emerald Betta
items.temperament: Males territorial toward other males; usually calmer than fancy bettas around other species
items.social: One male per tank, or a pair
items.diet: Carnivore: micro pellets, frozen and live foods such as daphnia, brine shrimp and bloodworms
items.note: A wild-type betta with a green-blue sheen and a more streamlined body than fancy bettas. It is a lovely planted-tank fish but is not as forgiving as the common betta, so give it clean, soft to moderate water, floating plants and an air gap under the lid.
tips: Keep one male per tank unless it is large and heavily planted.
Leave an air gap under the lid.
Offer frozen and live foods; wild-type bettas can be picky.

items.name: Mayan Cichlid
items.origin: Yucatan and Central America (Mexico to Nicaragua)
items.social: Solitary or a bonded pair in a large tank
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, frozen foods, earthworms, some vegetables
items.note: A hardy, brightly banded Central American cichlid that grows to about a foot and defends its space hard, especially when breeding. Give it a big tank, strong filtration and tough tankmates of similar size, and do not mix it with small fish.
tips: Plan for 75 gallons or more; larger for a pair with tankmates.
Do not keep with small fish or shrimp.
Use strong filtration and regular large water changes.

items.name: Banded Rainbowfish
items.diet: Omnivore: flakes, micro pellets, frozen and live foods
items.note: A hardy, active Australian rainbowfish with bold horizontal bands and colorful males. It likes a long tank, harder water and a group, and the males color up best when kept with several females.
tips: Keep six or more.
Use a long tank and a tight lid.
Prefers neutral to alkaline, moderately hard water.

items.name: Blue Badis
items.temperament: Peaceful but shy; males territorial toward each other
items.social: One male with a few females, or a pair
items.diet: Carnivore: live and frozen foods such as baby brine shrimp, bloodworms and daphnia
items.note: A small ambush hunter that slowly shifts color and likes to sit among plants and caves. It is more relaxed than a scarlet badis but still prefers live or frozen foods and a calm tank with hiding places.
tips: Stock live or frozen foods before buying; many refuse dry foods.
Provide caves and plants for male territories.
Keep with calm, small tankmates.

items.name: Amazon Puffer
items.origin: Amazon and Orinoco basins, South America
items.social: Small group in a roomy tank, or a single fish
items.diet: Carnivore: snails, frozen foods such as bloodworms and shrimp, small live foods
items.note: A black-and-white banded freshwater puffer that is one of the calmer puffers, but it is still a fin-nipper and a snail eater. Offer hard-shelled foods so its beak stays worn down, and keep it with fast, sturdy tankmates only.
tips: Feed snails or hard-shelled foods to keep the beak trimmed.
Keep away from long-finned or slow fish.
Needs very clean water; puffers are sensitive to nitrate.

items.name: Wolf Cichlid
items.origin: Atlantic and Pacific slopes of Costa Rica, Nicaragua and Honduras
items.social: Solitary, or a bonded pair in a very large tank
items.diet: Carnivore: large pellets, whole fish, shrimp, earthworms
items.note: One of the largest and most aggressive Central American cichlids. Juveniles look manageable, but adults can reach well over two feet, eat any fish that fits in the mouth and bully almost every tankmate, so it needs a tank of several hundred gallons and heavy filtration.
tips: Plan for 300 gallons or more before buying a juvenile.
Do not keep with small fish; large, tough tankmates only, and only in a very big tank.
Use a heavy lid and strong filtration; it is a messy eater.

items.name: T-Bar Cichlid
items.origin: Pacific slope of Costa Rica and Panama
items.diet: Omnivore: cichlid pellets, frozen foods, some vegetables
items.note: A small, striped Central American cichlid and a close relative of the convict cichlid. It is hardy but pairs defend a territory fiercely when breeding, so give it caves and keep it with sturdy tankmates.
tips: Provide caves and rockwork for a breeding pair.
Do not keep with small or shy fish.
Add one pair, not several fish, to a small tank.

items.name: Flier Cichlid
items.origin: Atlantic slope of Nicaragua and Costa Rica
items.diet: Omnivore leaning carnivore: pellets, frozen foods, worms
items.note: A flat-bodied, sunfish-like Central American cichlid that is calmer than most of its relatives outside breeding. It likes plants, caves and driftwood, and eats small fish and shrimp.
tips: Use plants, wood and caves for cover.
Keep with similar-sized, sturdy tankmates.
Do not mix with shrimp or tiny fish.

items.name: Red Cheek Tropheops
items.social: One male with several females, in a rock-heavy tank
items.diet: Mostly herbivore: spirulina flake and vegetable-based pellets, some frozen foods
items.note: A hardy Malawi mbuna with a red-orange wash on the cheek and a grazing, rock-hugging lifestyle. Like most mbuna it is pushy, so it does best in a rocky, hard-water tank stocked with other tough mbuna and extra females.
tips: Use hard, alkaline water and stacked rockwork.
Keep one male with several females to spread out aggression.
Feed a vegetable-based diet; too much meat causes bloat.

items.name: Electra Hap
items.diet: Omnivore leaning carnivore: pellets, spirulina flake, frozen foods
items.note: A calm, blue-and-silver open-water Malawi hap. Males show a bright blue-white head and a dark body when displaying. It is gentler than mbuna, but it needs a roomy tank and hard, alkaline water, and it will eat very small fish.
tips: Give it open swimming room as well as some rockwork.
Pair with other peaceful Malawi haps or mild mbuna, not very aggressive ones.
Keep one male with several females.

items.name: Featherfin Cichlid
items.temperament: Semi-peaceful; males display and chase each other
items.diet: Omnivore: spirulina flake, small pellets, frozen foods
items.note: A graceful Tanganyikan mouthbrooder. Males carry long, feather-like white tips on the pelvic fins and court females over a stone or flat rock. It is peaceful with fish its own size, but very hard, alkaline, clean water and a roomy tank are important.
tips: Give it a long tank with open water and some rockwork.
Keep one male with several females.
Do large weekly water changes and keep nitrate low.

items.name: Checkerboard Cichlid
items.origin: Rio Negro and nearby blackwater rivers, South America
items.social: One male with a few females
items.diet: Carnivore: small frozen foods, baby brine shrimp, micro pellets
items.note: A small, checker-marked dwarf cichlid from soft, acidic blackwater. It is peaceful and shy but fussy about water: San Diego tap water is hard, so most keepers mix it with RO water to get soft, acidic conditions.
tips: Use soft, acidic water, usually mixing RO or other soft water with tap.
Provide leaf litter, caves and plants.
Keep with small, calm tankmates only.

items.name: Nothobranchius Killifish
items.origin: Coastal East Africa (Kenya, Tanzania and Zanzibar)
items.temperament: Males squabble; mostly peaceful with other species
items.social: One male with two or three females
items.diet: Carnivore: frozen and live foods such as bloodworms, brine shrimp and daphnia, micro pellets
items.note: A brightly colored annual killifish that lives for only part of a year. Males are showy and bold, females plain. Species tanks work best; the fish live fast, breed on peat, and the eggs can rest dry for months.
tips: Keep one male with two or three females; males bicker.
Use a tight lid; they jump.
Expect a short life; this is natural for annual killifish.

items.name: Java Fern
items.propagation: Rhizome division, plantlets on old leaves
items.note: A tough, shade-tolerant fern that grows attached to wood or rock. Do not bury the rhizome, or it will rot.
tips: Tie or glue onto hardscape; do not plant in substrate.
Black spots on old leaves are normal.
Thrives in low light, great for beginners.

items.name: Anubias Nana
items.note: An exceptionally hardy, slow-growing plant with broad dark leaves. Keep the rhizome above the substrate, and keep algae off its slow leaves with lower light.
tips: Never bury the rhizome.
Lower light keeps algae off the leaves.
Good for fish that dig or nibble.

items.name: Java Moss
items.placement: Attach to wood, rock or mesh
items.note: A forgiving moss used for shrimp cover, fry cover and carpets. Trim regularly so it doesn't become a tangle.
tips: Tie to wood or rock with thread.
Great cover for shrimp and fry.
Trim to keep it neat and clean.

items.name: Amazon Sword
items.note: A big, classic centerpiece plant. A heavy root feeder, so give it a nutrient-rich substrate or root tabs.
tips: Use root tabs or rich substrate.
Needs room to grow upward.
Old leaves yellow and can be trimmed.

items.name: Vallisneria
items.note: A tall, grass-like plant that spreads by runners and tolerates hard, alkaline water well, which suits San Diego tap water.
tips: Plant in substrate, not the crown.
Spreads by runners; thin as needed.
Good for hard-water tanks.

items.name: Cryptocoryne Wendtii
items.note: A hardy, low-light rosette plant that comes in many colors. May 'melt' when moved, then regrow from the roots.
tips: Do not panic if leaves melt after planting.
Root tabs help it spread.
Leave it alone once settled.

items.name: Water Wisteria
items.note: A fast-growing, easy stem plant with lace-like or broad leaves depending on light. Good for soaking up excess nutrients.
tips: Trim and replant tops.
Bright light gives bushier growth.

items.name: Ludwigia Repens
items.note: A sturdy stem plant that turns red under strong light. Easy and fast-growing, and a great starter stem plant.
tips: Higher light brings out red tones.
Trim and replant the tops.

items.name: Rotala Rotundifolia
items.note: A fine-leaved stem plant that turns pink-orange in strong light. Responds well to CO2 and regular fertilizing.
tips: Needs steady fertilizers and light.
Trim often for dense bushes.

items.name: Bucephalandra
items.note: A slow, jewel-like epiphyte with iridescent leaves, used to detail hardscape. Attach to rock or wood and keep the rhizome clear of the substrate.
tips: Attach to hardscape.
Keep water stable; they are slow to adapt.
Do not bury the rhizome.

items.name: Monte Carlo
items.note: A low carpeting plant that makes a lush lawn under strong light and CO2. Needs bright light and a nutrient-rich substrate to stay compact.
tips: Plant in small clumps.
Needs strong light, CO2 and fertilizing.
Trim regularly to keep it dense.

items.name: Dwarf Hairgrass
items.note: A fine, grass-like carpet plant that spreads by runners. Needs bright light and trimming to stay low.
tips: Plant in small tufts.
Trim to keep it low.
Needs light, nutrients and patience.

items.name: Anacharis (Egeria)
items.note: A fast, cool-tolerant stem plant that absorbs nutrients quickly and helps keep algae in check. Also good for goldfish tanks, as it is cool-water tolerant (but goldfish may nibble it).
tips: Trim often; it grows fast.
Cool-water tolerant.
Float or plant in substrate.

items.name: Amazon Frogbit
items.note: A floating plant with trailing roots. Gives shade, cover for shy fish, and absorbs nutrients. Keep the leaves dry; they rot if constantly wet from a filter outlet.
tips: Keep the leaves dry from splashing.
Thin as needed.
Great for betta and shy fish tanks.

items.name: Bacopa Caroliniana
items.note: A forgiving stem plant with round leaves that turns bronze-pink under strong light.
tips: Plant stems in groups.
Trim the tops to bush out.

items.name: Red Ludwigia
items.note: A red-leaved stem plant that shows its best color under strong light and with iron-rich fertilizer.
tips: Strong light brings out red.
Trim tops and replant.

items.name: Alternanthera Reineckii
items.note: A reddish-purple stem plant, popular in colorful aquascapes. Needs good light and nutrients.
tips: Use strong light for color.
Replant trimmed tops.

items.name: Hygrophila
items.note: Fast-growing, hardy stem plants that help absorb excess nutrients. Several species are sold, including lancea and difformis.
tips: Trim often to keep it dense.
Easy for beginners.

items.name: Staurogyne Repens
items.note: A low, bushy plant that forms a lush carpet and is easier than many foreground plants.
tips: Trim to keep it low.
Moderate light is enough.

items.name: Pogostemon Helferi (Downoi)
items.note: A crinkled, low rosette plant that forms a carpet. Sensitive to rough planting and low nutrients.
tips: Plant gently.
Keep it well fed with root tabs.

items.name: Dwarf Baby Tears (HC Cuba)
items.note: A tiny-leaved, lush carpet plant that needs strong light and CO2 to stay low and dense.
tips: Needs strong light and CO2.
Plant in small portions.

items.name: Micro Sword
items.note: A grass-like carpet plant that spreads by runners when it gets light and nutrients.
tips: Plant in small clumps.
Needs strong light for a tight carpet.

items.name: Hornwort
items.note: A fast-growing, rootless plant that absorbs nutrients and shelters fry. It can shed needles when stressed.
tips: Float it or loosely anchor it.
Trim often.

items.name: Water Lettuce
items.note: A floating rosette with long roots that gives shade and cover. Keep the leaves dry and give it strong light.
tips: Keep leaves dry.
Needs strong light.

items.name: Salvinia
items.note: A tiny floating fern that spreads rapidly and shades the tank. Keep the leaves dry and thin it as needed. The aquarium trade sells dwarf species such as S. minima, S. natans and S. cucullata, which are distinct from the much larger giant salvinia (S. molesta/auriculata) that's federally and state regulated as a noxious aquatic weed.
tips: Keep leaves dry.
Thin regularly.
Never release any salvinia outdoors, even the dwarf trade species.

items.name: Red Root Floater
items.note: A floating plant whose roots and leaves turn red under bright light and with nutrient-rich water.
tips: Needs strong light for red color.
Keep leaves dry.

items.name: Christmas Moss
items.origin: Tropical regions (often sold as an Asian moss)
items.placement: Attach to wood or rock, carpet
items.note: A moss with a fir-tree look that makes a lush carpet or wall. Needs gentle trimming and clean water.
tips: Tie it to wood or rock.
Keep it clean of debris.

items.name: Marimo Moss Ball
items.note: A slow-growing green algae ball that is easy to keep. Roll it occasionally and keep it out of direct sun and hot water.
tips: Roll it now and then.
Keep it cool.

items.name: Java Fern Varieties
items.note: Java fern varieties such as narrow leaf, trident, windelov and lace share the same care as regular java fern. Attach them to hardscape and do not bury the rhizome. Taxonomists have also placed this species under Leptochilus pteropus, but Microsorum pteropus is still the name used nearly everywhere in the aquarium trade.
tips: Do not bury the rhizome.
Use thread or glue to attach.

items.name: Bolbitis
items.note: A slow, graceful fern that attaches to hardscape. Does best in stable, mature tanks.
tips: Do not bury the rhizome.
Be patient; it grows slowly.

items.name: Cryptocoryne Parva
items.note: A tiny crypt that carpets slowly. May melt after planting and regrow.
tips: Expect melt after planting.
Do not move it once settled.

items.name: Anubias Varieties
items.note: Anubias are very hardy, slow plants. Barteri, coffeefolia, petite, hastifolia, congensis, gigantea and others share the same care. Do not bury the rhizome.
tips: Do not bury the rhizome.
Keep leaves clear of algae with low-medium light.

items.name: Echinodorus Varieties
items.note: A large family of rosette plants including amazon sword, bleherae, ozelot, rose, red flame, marble queen and radican swords. All like rich substrate and root tabs.
tips: Feed with root tabs.
Trim old leaves.

items.name: Vallisneria Varieties
items.note: Easy, grass-like plants including corkscrew, jungle, giant and nana forms. Spread by runners to form a lush background.
tips: Keep crowns above the substrate.
Trim leaves as needed.

items.name: Aponogeton
items.note: Bulb plants with big, graceful leaves. Common types such as crispus and ulvaceus are fairly easy, but Madagascar lace is fussy and needs soft, clean, cooler water. They may go dormant and then regrow; do not discard the bulb.
tips: Do not bury the bulb fully.
Expect rest periods.
Madagascar lace plant is advanced: soft, slightly acidic, clean water and no heavy fertilizing.

items.name: Marsilea
items.note: A clover-leaf carpet plant that spreads in strong light.
tips: Needs strong light and nutrients.
Plant in small clumps.

items.name: Hydrocotyle (Pennywort)
items.note: Hardy pennywort species that create floating, carpeting or tall bush forms depending on type.
tips: Trim often.
Gives cover for fry.

items.name: Rotala Varieties
items.note: Colorful stem plants such as hra, macrandra, blood red, florida sunset and vietnam. Reward strong light and nutrients.
tips: Strong light brings out red and pink.
Trim and replant tops.

items.name: Ammannia
items.note: Colorful red stem plants such as bonsai, gracilis and sulawesi. Like strong light and steady nutrients.
tips: Needs strong light.
Trim and replant.

items.name: Eleocharis (Hairgrass)
items.note: Fine grass-like carpet plants. Need good light and nutrients to spread.
tips: Plant in small clumps.
Trim to keep it neat.

items.name: Guppy Grass
items.note: A delicate, fast-growing plant that hides fry and absorbs nutrients.
tips: Trim often.
Great for fry cover.

items.name: Parrot's Feather
items.note: A feathery plant that grows above water as well as below. Use caution in outdoor ponds because it can be invasive.
tips: Never release it outdoors.
Trim often.

items.name: Limnophila
items.note: Feathery, fast-growing stem plants such as sessiliflora and heterophylla that absorb nutrients quickly.
tips: Trim often.
Good for new tanks.

items.name: Mayaca
items.note: A fine-leaved moss-like stem plant that likes soft water and strong light.
tips: Needs strong light.
Trim and replant.

items.name: Tiger Lotus
items.note: A bulb plant with big, speckled leaves that can reach the surface. Trim floating leaves to let light through.
tips: Trim surface leaves.
Plant the bulb half-buried.

items.name: Pothos and Houseplants for Tanks
items.placement: Roots in water, leaves out of water
items.note: Pothos, philodendron and other houseplants can grow roots in aquarium water to absorb nutrients. Only the roots go in the water; the leaves stay in the air.
tips: Keep leaves above water.
Great for nitrate control.
aka: far east man plant pot holder

items.name: Bucephalandra Varieties
items.note: Slow, compact epiphytes with beautiful leaf colors and many named varieties, such as brownie, kedagang, godzilla and theia. Do not bury the rhizome.
tips: Do not bury the rhizome.
Stable water matters.

items.name: Anacharis
items.note: A fast, hardy stem plant that absorbs nutrients. Use caution outdoors; it can be invasive.
tips: Never release it outdoors.
Trim often.

items.name: Frogbit and Floaters
items.note: Floating plants that shade the tank and soak up nutrients. Keep leaves dry and thin them regularly.
tips: Thin regularly.
Keep leaves dry.

items.name: Tissue Culture Plants
items.note: Tissue culture plants are grown in sterile cups, so they come free of snails and pests. Rinse off the gel, divide into small plantlets, and plant them. Care follows the plant type.
tips: Rinse off all gel.
Divide into small portions and plant.

items.name: Dwarf Sagittaria
items.note: A grass-like plant that sends out runners and carpets the front of a tank. It grows taller in strong light, so trim to keep it low.
tips: Plant the crown at substrate level, not buried.
Root tabs help it spread.
Trim tall leaves to keep it as a carpet.

items.name: Water Sprite
items.note: A fast, feathery fern that soaks up nutrients quickly and gives fry and shy fish cover. It can be planted in the substrate or left floating.
tips: Remove or replant the baby plantlets that form on old leaves.
Floating plants soften the light for fish that like shade.
Trim often to keep it from shading other plants.

items.name: Cryptocoryne Balansae
items.note: A cryptocoryne with long, crinkled strap-like leaves. It may melt after planting, then regrow; leave it alone.
tips: Do not move it once planted.
Use root tabs.
Expect melt after changes.

items.name: Rotala Wallichii
items.note: A fine-leaved stem with a feathery look. It does best in soft water with CO2 and steady nutrients.
tips: Provide good light and CO2.
Trim tops and replant.
Keep water soft.

items.name: Ludwigia Arcuata
items.note: A needle-leaf stem plant with orange to red tones under bright light. It is easy to trim and replant.
tips: Use stronger light for color.
Trim and replant tops.
Keep it fed.

items.name: Bacopa Monnieri
items.note: A hardy stem plant with rounded leaves, sometimes called water hyssop. It adapts well and can grow above the water.
tips: Plant stems 1 inch apart.
Trim tops often.
Works in low-tech tanks.

items.name: Subwassertang
items.note: A feathery, moss-like fern. It is easy, drapes over wood and rock, and gives shrimp and fry cover.
tips: Tie to wood with thread.
Trim to shape.
Keep debris off it.

items.name: Duckweed
items.note: A tiny floating plant that doubles quickly and covers the surface. It shades tanks, removes nutrients and gives fry cover, but it is hard to remove once it spreads.
tips: Net out extra regularly; it can smother other floaters.
Keep it away from filters with strong surface agitation.
Choose it only if you want a dense surface cover.

items.name: Crinum (Onion Plant)
items.note: A bulb plant with long, wavy strap leaves that makes a bold specimen. It is a heavy root feeder and can grow very large, so it fits tanks with space and a deep substrate.
